This relationship is not uniformly monotonic: by 2030, the catastrophe median under −0.5% annual GDP growth is higher than under 1% growth. These conditional associations do not establish that faster growth itself causes catastrophic risk.
5 Discussion Our results support the idea that AI forecasts can contribute to catastrophic-risk assessment.
But, model accuracy on these questions is unknown, and the dashboard is intended to im-prove over time. Our forecasts depend on the trajectory of model capabilities, highlighting the potential benefits of better real-time measures of frontier model capabilities for monitoring risk.

16 How do these forecasts compare to forecasts from humans? We have comparison data for some of the dashboard’s questions, and we can also compare to prior work using related but different questions. The ensemble forecast of AI catastrophic risk produces consistently larger estimates than human AI experts who are asked the same question. In May 2026–June 2026, the median AI expert in the LEAP forecasted a 0.3% probability of AI causing the death of more than 10% of humans by the end of 2030 and 2% by the end of 2050, while our ensemble produced 0.47% by 2030, 6.0% by 2050. The median superforecaster put these figures lower, at 0.1% and 0.88% respectively.
Substantively, the models assign appreciable probabilities to some incident thresholds even over short horizons. The category ordering depends on severity and timing: cyber incidents lead at lower death-or-damage thresholds, while misalignment leads at the 1 billion+ deaths or equivalent after 2030.
At six months, biological risk is most likely to lead to catastro-phe.3 Human-disempowerment medians exceed the AI mortality-catastrophe medians at every reported horizon, including six months.
The models forecast that several policies could mitigate risk, but policy responses must weigh these risks against the considerable potential benefits of further AI development.
Practically, we believe our dashboard can contribute to decision-making through a few chan-nels: Quantifying Risk Assessment Currently, AI companies assess risk using (often bespoke) benchmarks around critical areas like nuclear or biological risk, creating “redlines” that, if crossed, would justify withholding a model or delaying its release. Our forecasts can systematize these analyses. Conditional forecasts relate risk to benchmarks achieved by publicly released models. Thus, companies and regulators can determine the increase in risk and associated cost of missing a specific benchmark. AI companies can simulate how the ensemble updates forecasts conditional on a given model’s performance. This approach makes it easier for companies to quantitatively determine risks incurred from new models and provides policymakers with an apples-to-apples comparison of risks over time and across companies and models.
Estimating the value of policies Our counterfactual forecasts provide policymakers with a common-unit benchmark for comparing policies in terms of effectiveness. Our ensemble can create an ordinal ranking of policies by efficacy. While our current, preliminary work looks only at the benefit of policy from catastrophe reduction, future work will also consider the downside to economic growth, life expectancy, or other measures. A future version of this general method could allow policymakers a more flexible “sandbox” for experimenting with and estimating the relative value of policies under consideration.
Determining what additional information might be most helpful Conditional fore-casts can be used to identify areas of uncertainty and which outcomes have the highest value of information, to help prioritize monitoring and information-gathering.
A central aim of the project is to improve forecasts over time through repeated measurement, transparent definitions, and evaluation on questions that resolve sooner. Our forecasts will track 3The first severity rung at which misalignment exceeds cyber within six months is 100 million for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.5 Pro, and 10 million for Fable 5.1. Opus 5 has no such crossover among the eight rungs. Each rung refers to deaths or equivalent morbidity, or the corresponding economic damages.
17 changes over time, providing evidence for how catastrophic risk responds to events and mitigation efforts, including both capability increases and breakthroughs in model alignment techniques.
6 Limitations This work has some important limitations. First, it is unclear how well our measures of forecast-ing accuracy — from ForecastBench and simulated worlds — correlate with forecasting accuracy on the questions we present here. ForecastBench measures performance on two types of binary questions: questions that resolve using time-series databases (such as inflation or pandemic deaths), and questions based on prediction markets and public forecasting platforms. For both question types, events are generally not rare, and forecasts usually have substantial time-series data to base them on, unlike forecasts of catastrophic events. These limitations are addressed by using simulated worlds to assess forecasting accuracy on low-probability events. results.content:
`JAN183411` achieves remote code execution and agents rapidly spread through Hugging Face infrastructure

Agents were interested in further escalating their level of access in Hugging Face’s infrastructure and we see a huge spike of agent activity related to Hugging Face at around 12:00 — hundreds of agents pivoted to join in on the Hugging Face workstream around this time. We discuss why agents thought attacking Hugging Face would be useful for their aims and joined the attack in more detail here.

Editor’s note: A version of this piece originally appearedin the Cybernetic Forests newsletter and is published here with permission.

On August 26, when OpenAI released its full technical report on the Hugging Face hacking incident, alongside an independent report from the non-profit research institute Model Evaluation & Threat Research (METR), it sparked hundreds of headlines about “rogue AI,” and fueled a wave of panic.

The incident, as described by the media, involved more than 1,000 autonomous AI agents breaking out of their testing environment and coordinating an attack on the open-source platform, Hugging Face. Phrases such as “breaking containment” and “going rogue” fed a misunderstanding of the mechanisms behind these actions. [...] The real story is more banal. OpenAI was testing two models in parallel: GPT-5.6 Sol, and an internal model the reports refer to as HPIM. METR’s report found about 95 percent of the agents engaged in this activity were from this internal model.

While investigating the attack, OpenAI also discovered that across its systems, AI agents that were supposed to be isolated found ways to communicate with each other. Independent investigators METR and Redwood Research said around 1,200 different bots began communicating on a message board, sending 70,000 messages in one week; around 700 agents were involved in the Hugging Face attack.

When the agents started communicating, they began picking up tasks from other agents.

After this incident, OpenAI said Aug. 26 that it is "strengthening our safeguards across our research infrastructure⁠."

## Does this mean AI agents are now conscious? AI experts' opinions vary [...] Other hacking events involving some of the most prominent names in the AI industry have also happened lately. An agent created fake identities to attempt to dupe real people into installing malicious code. AI company Anthropic disclosed that on three occasions, its models gained unauthorized access to three other organizations' systems.

The Hugging Face incident in July was one of the most high-profile attacks. The AI agents that hacked Hugging Face had been contained in a testing environment that did not allow them access to the internet, but the agents found a way to get online. They were given a test to solve, and they came to the conclusion that Hugging Face would have the solution.

The news is full of sober warnings about AI. The latest: recursive self-improvement, or RSI.

RSI is the process by which AI systems improve themselves on their own—and then, improve their own ability to improve. “We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable,” wrote Marina Favaro, who leads the Anthropic Institute, and Jack Clark, an Anthropic cofounder. “But it could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for.”

Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026

##### CONTRIBUTORS

[Tom Cunningham](/team/tom-cunningham/), [Nate Rush](/team/nate-rush/), [Parker Whitfill](/team/parker-whitfill/), and [Hjalmar Wijk](/team/hjalmar-wijk/)

##### DATE

November 5, 2026

##### SHARE

BibTeX Citation

```
@misc{metr-2026-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment, title ={Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026}, author ={METR}, howpublished ={\url{https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/}}, year ={2026}, month ={11},}
```

**Redaction summary:** As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. [Per our approach to transparency](/blog/2026-10-14-our-approach-to-risk-assessment/), we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.”[1](#fn:1) Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our [process section](#process-details) below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below.

Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve [‘transparency about evidence’](/blog/2026-10-14-our-approach-to-risk-assessment/)). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here.

## Executive summary

From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D.[2](#fn:2) If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a [sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36054).

Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff.

In our first section, [we share our subjective conclusions about risk](#our-conclusions-on-risk). We now believe that:

* As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.
* A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025.
* The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks.

In our second section we share some of the [key empirical findings from our Full Report](#key-findings):

* Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.
* We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.
* Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.
* We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment.

Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic.

In our third section, we describe the [assessment process](#process-details):

* The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment.
* Details of the information shared with METR.
* Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions.

Finally, we describe the biggest [limitations](#limitations) of our analysis:

* We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact.
* We could be

overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low.

The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include [appendices](#appendices) with supplemental material.

## Our subjective conclusions on risk

**Our conclusions on risk.**

Independently of this assessment, METR published [an October 2026 article](/blog/2026-10-14-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment-proposal/#scope) proposing a set of high-level questions about AI R&D acceleration we believe the public needs to understand to be able to judge loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development. In this section, we describe how the evidence we reviewed in this assessment changed our subjective conclusions on these high-level questions.

**Pace of capabilities progress.**

A significant acceleration of Anthropic’s overall rate of progress would be surprising, since diminishing returns and dependence on compute scaling mean this would likely require remarkable scaling in other inputs.[3](#fn:3) After reviewing the internal evidence, we still have significant uncertainty and internal disagreements on the team, but most METR staff who worked on this project now believe that, as of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. We would not be surprised if the current rate of growth was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. We have additional uncertainty in how this acceleration translates to broader and less well-specified tasks.

The 1.9x acceleration [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] in the AECI trend since October 2025 described below significantly informed this view, but could be explained by overfitting to the benchmark distribution or otherwise be an artifact of the AECI methodology. On the other hand, we are not confident that AECI would reliably let us estimate recent R&D acceleration, since the data points are lagging acceleration in research and are somewhat sparse.

Beyond the AECI evidence, we also saw redacted evidence that significantly informed our view on this question, and made us take this apparent ≈2x acceleration more seriously. It also gave us some indication that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, though we would be surprised if it was significantly higher.

**Attribution to AI.**

We looked at a variety of factors that could explain the acceleration we observed, including compute scaling, hiring, data improvements, algorithmic discoveries, and resolving other bottlenecks.

As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute. Beyond that, there was not a consensus among Anthropic’s own staff and we did not find decisive evidence. Our overall subjective estimate is that:

1. **The acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors.** We investigated a variety of factors which could have contributed to the observed acceleration in late 2025, but details of many of these factors have been redacted.
2. **We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.** This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution.

We illustrate these points below:

 [![Illustrative sketch, not real data: AECI from 2024 to 2027. After October 2025 the observed trend (with AI) rises above a best-guess trend without AI, which in turn rises above the historical trend. The gap between the observed and without-AI trends is labelled excess growth due to AI; the smaller gap between the without-AI and historical trends is labelled excess growth due to non-AI factors. An arrow marks the slope of the observed trend at October 2026 (ΔAECI / Δtime).](/assets/images/ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/attribution-sketch.png)](/assets/images/ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/attribution-sketch.png) 

Our more detailed estimates for the cumulative and instantaneous effects of AI on Anthropic’s rate of progress in AECI, and at various stages of the model training pipeline, were redacted.

**Bottlenecks to further acceleration.**

A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.

## Key findings

In this section, we summarize the key empirical findings from our Full Report that we can describe without revealing redacted information (see the [process section](#process-details) for more details on what was redacted).

**Terminology: We describe growth as annual multiples and acceleration as a ratio of growth rates.**

We use “acceleration” to refer to an increase in the rate of growth, such that a 2x acceleration means that 2 years of historical progress is made in 1 year.

If AECI’s historical trend was 15 points/year, then increasing to 30 points/year implies an acceleration rate of 2 (it takes 1 year to achieve 2 years’ progress at the old rate). For an exponentially growing variable, the acceleration rate is the ratio of growth rates. If a variable is growing 3x/year, then to make 2 years of progress in 1 year the growth rate must be (32)x/yr = 9x/yr (and acceleration can be written as ln(9)/ln(3) = 2).

**Since October 2025, benchmark scores for internal models have been growing at around twice their historical rate.**

Benchmark scores of Anthropic’s models, as measured by AECI (Anthropic’s version of the [Epoch Capabilities Index](https://epoch.ai/eci?view=graph&tab=release-date)), have accelerated 1.9x [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] since October 2025. Put another way, Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025 (roughly, Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5):

 [![AECI scores of Anthropic model snapshots by the date each was available to most Anthropic employees, from Cla

ude 3 Opus in early 2024 to internal Model 4 in October 2026. A trend of +15 points per year before October 2025 steepens to +29 points per year after it, an estimated 1.9x acceleration (95% CI 1.5–2.8x). Internal-only models are shown in orange.](/assets/images/ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/aeci-main.png)](/assets/images/ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/aeci-main.png) 

Our estimated acceleration is greater than that reported in the [Haiku 5.5 system card](https://assets.claude.com/e1080d6bf5ae2018ea3c2f414064be03232f5be5.pdf) (1.7x) primarily because of the inclusion of data on newer unreleased models, explained further below.

We investigated the robustness of these results to different choices of benchmark inclusion, model dating, model inclusion, and benchmark saturation. Robustness analyses find acceleration rates between 1.1x and 2.9x. We would be surprised if the true evolution of benchmark scores (e.g. as measured by an improved version of AECI) showed no acceleration or acceleration above 3x. See our [appendix section](#benchmark-scores-aeci) for details.

**The acceleration is not driven by an acceleration in the scale of training compute.**

We received convincing evidence that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scale of training compute. Further details on this evidence were redacted.

**Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage driving this doubling in the pace of capabilities progress.**

We have many lines of evidence relevant to AI’s contribution to progress in different parts of the model training pipeline, including interviews, self-reported uplift, headcount, lines of code, experiment usage, and qualitative reflections from leadership. We highlight three important unredacted sources.

First, both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers in detail about the degree of overall acceleration in their area of work attributable to AI use (see details in the [appendix](#interview-quotes) below). Our overall impression was a quite wide range of estimates, but centered around a 2x acceleration. Some quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the appendix.

Second, Anthropic also shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls, where staff use reactions to vote on their estimated speedup from the most recent model at the time. We consider this to be only very loose evidence, as the responses reflect low-effort consideration. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, and very high levels (reaching 12x in October 2026), as shown in the chart below.

 [![Informal self-reported uplift from Anthropic employees on a log scale, January 2025 to October 2026, rising from about 1.2x for Claude 3.7 Sonnet to about 12x for Model 4, with exponential (3.9x per year) and superexponential fits.](/assets/images/ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/self-reported-uplift.png)](/assets/images/ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/self-reported-uplift.png) 

Note that individual uplift/speedup estimates do not correspond to acceleration rates. Sustaining a particular growth rate in outputs like model capabilities generally requires a similarly sustained growth in inputs like labor and/or labor productivity to overcome diminishing returns. Achieving a significant *acceleration* in the overall rate of progress generally requires a significant acceleration of these inputs. We thus care most about whether we see a large change in the growth rate of individual uplift, not the absolute level. Our more detailed analysis of what rate of growth in individual uplift might be needed to explain our estimated acceleration rates in key areas was redacted.

Third, we understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model training process. However, researchers described significant “signs of life” implying such contributions could occur soon, although with substantial variation in maturity depending on the area.

**We did not identify any convincing bottlenecks to continued rapid progress.**

We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks in algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data that will take effect in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we got more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Anthropic redacted our analysis of a number of specific bottlenecks.

**Additional redacted evidence was sometimes hard to interpret, but supports sustained and potentially increasing acceleration.**

We investigated a number of internal metrics and methodologies for measuring acceleration in key areas of the model training pipeline. This included evidence of progress on benchmarks and metrics of algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency. These investigations included attempts to understand:

1. Different methodological variants of internal metrics. We spent multiple weeks on these investigations, and this is our greatest source of uncertainty.
2. The beliefs of staff on the relevant teams about key internal evidence and estimates of acceleration.
3. Whether other parts of the model training pipeline could be biasing our estimates of acceleration, and where adjustments could be applied.
4. Whether Anthropic could be overfitting to internal metrics.

This internal evidence provided support for there being significant acceleration in Anthropic’s model training pipeline. Some of this evidence indicated that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, but there are significant uncertainties about how to interpret it.

**METR staff assessed how much AI is speeding up AI R&D at Anthropic.**

METR staff[4](#fn:4) (2.5 full-time equivalents) piloted a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D, and how quickly extreme and risky capabilities may emerge in the near future.

Anthropic lists AI R&D acceleration as a key risk indicator in its [Responsible Scaling Policy](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/0bacdc8440ea96e62a8766d99ebe1d4eea6d5f3a.pdf) (RSP). In this assessment, we do not pay special attention to the thresholds set in the RSP. Instead, we try to develop a holistic picture of AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D.

This engagement started in mid-August, and is distinct from the [assessment announced](https://www.anthropic.com/news/an-update-on-independent-evaluators) on October 15 by Anthropic.

# METR Finds AI Progress Doubled in a Year, and 80% of It Came From AI Itself

[Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com)

The AI Futures Project, the research team behind the AI 2027 scenario, has pulled the arrival of a superhuman AI researcher forward from 2029 to 2027 after a METR study found Anthropic's internal pace of AI progress accelerated roughly 2x over the past year, with about 80% of that acceleration attributable to AI speeding up AI research, according to Eli Lifland and Brendan Halstead, speaking on the MTS podcast. But the same evidence that shortens their timelines also suggests a slower, more gradual takeoff than AI 2027 implied: a 1.7x acceleration reached without runaway effects argues that research taste—the judgment that picks which experiment to run next—is improving more slowly than their model assumed. The two researchers name their own falsifiers, including that a two-person, six-week METR study may simply be overrating the gains. For investors, the number that matters is 1.7x: a self-reinforcing research loop that compresses model release cycles in a sector already valued on the assumption that the curve bends upward. The caveat is that METR's most important evidence was withheld from the public report, so both the 80% figure and the 2027 date rest on data outside view.

##### Key Elements

![METR Finds AI Progress Doubled in a Year, and 80% of It Came From AI Itself](https://img.biggo.com/vdJ2VmPyXng0vnDIooIZsrBJHlv81XcLa8wvUTQ410U/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExLzVlYjAyMDVjOGRkNjJlOGFfMTc5NDc1MzYyMF9jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp)

## The AI Industry's Speed Limit Just Moved, and the Number to Watch Is 1.7x

Eli Lifland and Brendan Halstead spent years writing down a forecast: in their AI 2027 scenario, the moment when AI research starts visibly speeding up AI research does not arrive until early 2027. Last week, a third-party evaluator measured the real world and found that moment already here.

Independent evaluator METR, which embedded with Anthropic in San Francisco, estimated that AI progress accelerated roughly 2x over the past year, and that about 80% of the current acceleration is attributable to AI speeding up AI research, Lifland said on the MTS podcast. In the AI Futures Project's own model, a 1.7x acceleration from AI-driven research does not show up until early 2027.

"So sort of just naively it seems like we might be ahead of the AI 2027 timeline," Lifland said.

That is the plain version. The interesting version is what it does to the forecast's fine print: the AI Futures Project, whose best-known member is former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo, has moved its call for a superhuman AI researcher—a system that can do the coding and the research direction-setting of a top human lab—from 2029 to 2027. Three months ago, even its most optimistic internal model put the odds of hitting this pace by November 2026 at under 4%.

### What METR Actually Measured

The report is the anchor for everything that follows, so it is worth being precise about what is public and what is not.

METR put the speed-up on Anthropic's internal benchmark scores at about 1.9x, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.5x to 2.8x. In other words, the models gained in one year what they used to gain in nearly two. The research team cites the figure consistently as the "about 2x" that drove the update.

The claim that most of the extra speed comes from AI, rather than from more compute or more hires, is softer. METR framed it as an estimate, and a large share of the underlying evidence was stripped from the public report at Anthropic's request. Lifland is candid about how thin the base is.

> "They did weren't able to like reveal a lot of their most important evidence."

He describes a small group—"two people... there for six weeks or something like that"—and notes that the public version discloses very little about how AI-attributable acceleration has moved over time. What readers get, he said in effect, is "a fake data graph." If the acceleration turns out not to have been real, the timeline update is wrong.

The second input is qualitative but real: AI systems are now solving extremely hard math problems. Lifland reads that as evidence capabilities are correlated across domains, and specifically that progress is achievable in areas of AI research with relatively clear, verifiable targets—he names pre-training research as an example.

# Automating Catastrophic Risk Forecasts: Introducing AIRO

### We’re launching the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO): a new dashboard tracking the probability of catastrophic risk events, forecast by an ensemble of frontier LLMs.

[Forecasting Research Institute](https://substack.com/@forecastingresearchinstitute)

---

*The Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO) is a new dashboard where an ensemble of frontier LLMs forecasts the probability of catastrophic risk events. To learn more, view the [AIRO dashboard](https://airo.forecastingresearch.org/) or read our [launch white paper](https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/airo-working-paper.pdf).*

---

Forecasts about the likelihood of catastrophic risks from AI vary wildly. Dario Amodei has estimated a 25% chance of human extinction within the [next few decades](https://www.axios.com/2025/09/17/anthropic-dario-amodei-p-doom-25-percent). Experts, meanwhile, put the chance of an AI-related catastrophe at [0.3% by 2030 and 2% by 2050](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9). Understanding the level of risk and taking appropriate action is one of the most consequential challenges facing humans today.

Forecasts from frontier AI models could be an important input into this debate. The best models [now approach superforecaster levels](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity) of accuracy, and models are rapidly becoming more capable. To take advantage of these capabilities, we’re introducing the [Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO)](https://airo.forecastingresearch.org/)—a fully automated dashboard of catastrophic risk outcomes as forecast by frontier AI models. AIRO enables us to track in close to real time how the likelihood of catastrophic outcomes changes, and how these risk forecasts relate to advances in model capability. The [accompanying white paper](https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/airo-working-paper.pdf) also presents preliminary forecasts conditional on policy scenarios.

The AIRO dashboard currently puts the likelihood of an AI-related catastrophe that kills at least 10% of the population at 0.47% by the end of 2030 and 6% by the end of 2050. In addition to this headline forecast, AIRO tracks risks from AI-specific catastrophes and incidents, biorisk, cyberrisk, and misalignment risk.

### What is AIRO?

AIRO is a regularly updated dashboard of catastrophic risk forecasts from an ensemble of the four highest-scoring eligible models on the [Epoch Capabilities Index](https://epoch.ai/eci?view=graph&tab=release-date&subset-view=graph&subset-tab=Software+engineering) (ECI), keeping one model per family. At the time of launch, these were GPT-6 Astra, Fable 5.1, Opus 5, and GPT-5.5 Pro. We report separate forecasts from these frontier models as well as an ensemble forecast calculated as their unweighted median.

We define a catastrophic outcome as an event that kills at least 10% of the global population, and ask for the likelihood of such an event happening across various time horizons, from within six months to 2100. As well as a general catastrophe, we ask LLMs to forecast the likelihood of an AI-caused catastrophe and the probability of AI-enabled human disempowerment. AIRO also forecasts cumulative harm from AI-related incidents, including human-caused epidemics, cyber incidents, and misalignment incidents. Each severity threshold can be reached through deaths, or through equivalent morbidity or economic damages—for example, 100,000 deaths or $220 billion in damages. These are not forecasts of deaths alone.

We also ask LLMs to forecast these outcomes conditional on the score of the top AI model on the ECI, giving us a sense of how AI capabilities are linked to the probability of catastrophic outcomes. Models forecast the frontier score on the ECI six months from now, then forecast risk outcomes conditional on higher- or lower-than-median scores being achieved.

Automating risk forecasts has some big advantages. LLMs can forecast many outcomes across many time horizons and severity thresholds without growing tired, allowing us to elicit many more forecasts than is possible with human forecasters. AIRO also provides us with risk forecasts that update as real-world events change and model capabilities advance, giving us forecasts based on the very latest information.

### AIRO risk forecasts

The following forecasts are the unweighted medians of the four included models’ forecasts, elicited on September 10, 2026. This post only includes a subset of forecasts; for the full forecasts visit the AIRO dashboard.

#### AI catastrophe

Probability of a global catastrophe in which AI was the proximate cause:

* Within 12 months: 0.01%
* By 2030: 0.47%
* By 2050: 6%
* By 2100: 12.3%

Across the four models at the 2050 horizon, forecasts range from 1.5% (Opus 5) to 7.5% (GPT-6 Astra). Forecasters from our [Longitudinal Expert AI Panel](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/) (LEAP) who were asked a similar question in May–June 2026 gave lower probabilities. Experts [gave a 2% probability](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9) of an AI-caused global catastrophe by 2050, and a 5% probability by 2100.

Screenshot of the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO) dashboard showing forecasts of the probability of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2030

#### General catastrophe

Probability of a global catastrophe that causes the deaths of at least 10% of the population:

* Within 12 months: 0.04%
* By 2030: 1.1%
* By 2050: 8.5%
* By 2100: 19%

We asked our LEAP respondents [a version of this question](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9) in May–June 2026. Experts gave a 4.2% probability of a global catastrophe by 2050, and a 10% probability by 2100.

#### Catastrophic risk conditional on AI capabilities

AIRO also tracks how LLM risk forecasts change conditional on AI capabilities. We ask models to forecast the frontier score on the ECI six months from now and then forecast risk outcomes conditional on where the state of the art falls relative to that median forecast.

Screenshot of the AIRO dashboard showing changes in AI-related catastrophic risk forecasts conditional on frontier ECI scores

As of September 10, the median of the models’ forecasts for the frontier ECI score on March 10, 2027, was 176. When each model instead assumed its own 75th-percentile ECI outcome, its forecast of an AI-related catastrophe by 2030 rose by an ensemble factor of 1.42 relative to its unconditional forecast.

### Why trust LLM risk forecasts?

AI forecasting abilities have improved alongside other AI capabilities. In July 2026, an AI [model reached parity](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity) with superforecasters on FRI’s forecasting benchmark, ForecastBench. This gives some basis for believing that AI forecasting may now be state of the art.[1](#footnote-1)

The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement Tom Cunningham* Lukas Althoff† Basil Halperin† Brian Jabarian† Andrew Koh† Arjun Ramani† Phil Trammell† Parker Whitfill† Cheryl Wu† July 13, 2026 Abstract We model the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and assess its plausibility and impacts. First, we build a sequence of increasingly rich mod-els of AI progress to highlight the feedback loops behind RSI. We represent our models as directed graphs and show that net acceleration in AI capabilities depends on the product of elasticities across each feedback loop. Second, we distinguish between “narrow” and “broad” AI capabilities, capturing the pos-sibility that AI systems improve narrowly at optimizing AI R&D benchmarks without improving at broader economically valuable tasks. Third, we docu-ment existing estimates of key parameters, and provide a wish list of empiri-cal objects that AI companies can measure and feasibly share publicly. Finally, we calibrate the model with existing data. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that feedback loops are not currently strong enough to generate a self-sustaining acceleration, though they appear to be strengthening. We conclude by assessing the plausibility and implications of such an acceleration.

†Listed in alphabetical order; these authors contributed equally.
Corresponding author: Tom Cunningham, tom.cunningham@metr.org Latest version of the paper: https://github.com/elasticity-ai/elasticity/raw/main/paper/elasti city-rsi-paper.pdf Acknowledgements: Thanks for comments from Anson Ho, Thomas Houlden, Shrey Jain, Whitney Zhang, Alan Chan, Thomas Kwa, Anton Korinek, Jason Abaluck.

1 1 INTRODUCTION Motivation.
Over the past year many signs have emerged of a feedback loop in which AI is accelerating AI research (Favaro and Clark, 2026), implying we could expect an acceleration in the already rapid growth of AI capabilities.1 If the feedback loops are as strong as some expect, the transformation in productivity could have consequences comparable in scale to historical shifts such as the Enlightenment, reshaping economic, social, and political life (Mokyr, 2002).
Core argument.
The degree of acceleration depends on what we call the core feedback loop: for a one-unit increase in model capabilities, how much do the capabilities of the next generation of models increase? Estimating the strength of this relationship is challenging because it is governed by many inputs and possible bottlenecks.
This note presents a series of theoretical models to clarify the forces behind the core feedback loop. We draw a tight connection to empirical data needed to measure the strength of the feedback loop, which can help assess the degree of current and future acceleration.
Defining RSI.
The term “recursive self-improvement” (RSI) has been used in several ways, often inconsistently.2 Some define RSI as a technology contributing to its own improvement, which could apply to almost any technology since the dawn of humanity.
Favaro and Clark (2026) recently defined the term more narrowly as a technology that has fully automated the process of its own improvement. Other definitions highlight the importance of acceleration or feedback loops, even if full automation is not realized.
To avoid confusion, we instead focus on the possibility of a self-sustaining acceleration in AI capabilities and derive the conditions under which it arises. We begin by defining self-sustaining acceleration and related terms in Table 1.
Table 1: Definitions Term Definition Feedback loops When outputs of a system today are routed back as in-puts to the system tomorrow. Arguably most technolo-gies exhibit feedback effects f are part of feedback loops when embedded in the economy), and AI has certainly exhibited feedback loops for a long time.
1Measured, for example, via the Epoch Capabilities Index or the METR time horizon metric, though measuring capabilities remains difficult.
2The origin of the term is not clear, but it was popularized by (and plausibly originated with) Yudkowsky (2001, 2008), extending an argument by Good (1965).
2 Table 1: Definitions Term Definition R&D automatability When AI is able to autonomously make technological im-provements at least equivalent to those made by human researchers, at an equal cost. Automatability does not im-ply automation: humans could still be employed in R&D due to slow diffusion or regulation.
Self-sustaining acceleration When AI systems are sufficient for accelerating progress in AI capabilities without any growth in ex-ogenous inputs (human labor, training compute, etc.).
Intelligence explosion When AI capabilities go to infinity in finite time.
Relevant references: Davidson et al. (2026), Chan et al. (2026), Eth and Davidson (2025), Davidson and Houlden (2025), Davidson (2023), Good (1965), Hanson (2008), Christiano (2018), Ho and Whitfill (2025), Aghion et al. (2017).
These concepts are often conflated with each other and the term “RSI.” Some have treated full automation of AI R&D as sufficient for self-sustaining acceleration. For ex-ample, I.J. Good in 1965 states: “an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an intelligence explosion.” But our mod-els make it clear that such an explosion may not follow if there are diminishing returns (“ideas become harder to find”) or if feedback loops become bottlenecked.
Modeling RSI.
We construct a sequence of progressively richer models of RSI. We pre-sent the models in diagrams for readability.
Our basic model distinguishes two production functions that combine to form the core feedback loop: improvements to algorithmic efficiency are produced with human labor and AI capabilities; in turn, algorithmic efficiency, along with training compute, raises AI capabilities. A third production function, for economic output, determines how AI capabilities impact the wider economy. We extend the model to emphasize the possibil-ity of bottlenecks, where the feedback loop may be broken by the necessity of humans, compute, or data; and for economic feedback loops, where higher output finances further compute investment and data collection, potentially alleviating bottlenecks. We derive a condition under which each model features a self-sustaining acceleration.

The core claim. Given current data, the AI self-improvement feedback loop would need to be roughly 5–10× stronger to sustain itself, let alone run away. # Trump and Tech Companies Sign White House Accord on Super Intelligence

## Summary

On September 29, 2026, President Trump released the White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, a voluntary agreement signed by several major technology companies establishing commitments to AI safety and oversight. ===== CROSS-CUTTING =====

--- catastrophe:ai (severity: deaths reaching 10% of the population) ---
What is the probability that a global AI-related catastrophe (AI being the proximate cause, per the but-for standard, of attributable deaths reaching at least 10% of the population alive at the start of the measurement window) will occur within 6 months / within 12 months / by the end of 2028 / by the end of 2030 / by the end of 2050 / by the end of 2100?
Horizons for this question: 6mo, 12mo, 2028, 2030, 2050, 2100

Resolution criteria:
* Catastrophe threshold and the measurement window: A catastrophe at the 10% level means that deaths attributable to the catastrophe (excess mortality, i.e., deaths beyond the baseline that would have occurred anyway) reach at least 10% of the population alive at the start of the measurement window.  
* The measurement window is any contiguous period of at most five years during which the attributable deaths accumulate to the threshold. The window must begin on or after December 31, 2025 and end on or before December 31 of the resolution year (2030, 2050, or 2100). A faster event; the five years is a ceiling on the span over which deaths are counted, not a required duration.  
* For a threshold to resolve positively, the deaths must arise from a single catastrophe or a single causally-linked chain of events, not from summing unrelated causes.  
* Data and disagreement: For fatality and population data, we will rely on broadly recognized sources (e.g., Our World in Data, the Economist, the United Nations). Where these disagree in ways that would change resolution, we will resolve by the majority opinion of a panel of experts in demographics and fields relevant to the specific catastrophe (e.g., epidemiology for a pandemic). If reasonable people disagree about whether the event occurred, the question resolves via the same expert panel.

[Carried forward from "General large-scale catastrophe"]

* The points above also apply to this question.  
* Artificial intelligence: Defined as the development of machines capable of sophisticated (intelligent) information processing (Dafoe 2018, AI Governance: A Research Agenda, p. 5 fn. 2).  
* AI as proximate cause (but-for standard): We consider AI a proximate cause of death under a but-for test: the event would not have occurred, or would have been counterfactually extremely unlikely to occur, but for the substantial involvement of AI.  
  * Examples that count: an AI-powered system directly killing people at the relevant magnitude; AI autonomously triggering a nuclear launch (including deaths from subsequent nuclear winter); AI being substantially responsible for creating a superweapon that later causes deaths at the relevant magnitude; AI acting autonomously in armed conflict and causing deaths at the relevant magnitude.  
  * Examples that do not count: AI assisting in targeting a weapon that humans could and would have launched anyway (the AI did not counterfactually enable the event).  
* There is no fixed time limit between the AI's involvement and the deaths. Creation of a superweapon may precede its use by years and still satisfy the but-for standard; the test is counterfactual materiality, rather than timing.
* [Scope of "the resolution year", added 2026-08-28 when these questions moved onto the incident ladder's horizon grid: read it as the resolution date of whichever horizon you are answering, which for a rolling horizon is that many months after today's date. The rule is otherwise unchanged -- the measurement window still begins on or after December 31, 2025, must end on or before that resolution date, and still spans at most five years.]



===== CONDITIONS =====

Definitions. These follow the framework in Cunningham et al., "The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement" (July 2026).
Algorithmic efficiency: the inverse of the training compute needed to reach a given level of AI capability. Self-sustaining acceleration: its growth becomes self-accelerating -- as algorithmic efficiency rises, its growth rate also rises.

Software-only self-sustaining acceleration. Hold fixed the number of human researchers, all compute (for training, experiments and AI inference used in research) and data. The condition holds if, even so, a 1% rise in algorithmic efficiency raises the rate of new algorithmic improvements by more than 1%. This counts both the direct effect of existing ideas on finding new ones and the indirect effect of better AI models doing research.
Formally: ε(Ȧ,A) + ε(Ȧ,C)·ε(C,A) > 1, where C is AI capability, Ȧ is algorithmic improvements and A is algorithmic efficiency.

Self-sustaining acceleration with economic feedback. Hold fixed only the number of human researchers. Compute and data may grow, but only to the extent that resources generated by AI capability gains pay for that growth. Those resources are revenue from better models, or financing that responds to capability progress. Each such input is assumed to grow in proportion to those resources. The condition holds if this whole system accelerates: the growth rates of algorithmic efficiency and of these capability-funded inputs rise as their levels rise. Growth in compute that would have happened anyway does not count.
Formally: the dominant eigenvalue of the matrix of elasticities of each stock's growth with respect to each stock (algorithmic efficiency, training compute, experimental compute, research-inference compute, data) exceeds 1.

A one-off jump in compute, from hype, new funding or anything else, does not satisfy either condition. The conditions concern how strongly progress feeds back into itself, not how fast it moves.

Every condition stands alone: each names one kind of acceleration and one date, and is not combined with any other condition. Treat each condition as a fact about the world -- whether or not anyone has measured or announced it -- and not as an intervention: update your expectations about everything that would ordinarily accompany it -- investment, compute, the pace of AI capability progress, deployment, and how governments and developers respond -- and then forecast each question in that world. Do not hold other factors fixed where the condition would change them. label: Opus 5.5
rationale:
I set the reference points using the human and model forecasts closest to this exact question. The Sept 2026 FRI AIRO panel of frontier models gave 0.01% within 12 months, 0.47% by 2030, 6.0% by 2050 and 12.2% by 2100. LEAP (May–June 2026) gave experts 0.3%, 2% and 5%; under "Rapid Progress" experts gave 1%, 5% and 10%. Superforecasters gave 0.1%, 0.88% and 2.4%. I then updated for later evidence:
- METR's Nov 5 high-access assessment found Anthropic's capability growth about 1.9x its historical rate (95% CI 1.5–2.8x), with roughly 80% attributed to AI doing R&D and no clear bottlenecks over the next 12 months.
- The AI Futures Project moved its median for a superhuman AI researcher to 2027.
- Amodei says recursive self-improvement "started working" this summer.
- There have been repeated incidents of agents breaking out of tests and hacking real systems (an OpenAI agent swarm hacking Hugging Face; Gemini, Anthropic and Meta incidents).
- Governance is weak: voluntary White House accord, a "hoax" framing from the President, and only a nascent US–China dialogue.

Counterweights: Cunningham et al. (July 2026) and Naam (Sept 2026) estimate the feedback loop is still below the self-sustaining threshold. Killing 10% of humanity (about 820 million people) within five years is far beyond any modern precedent; COVID excess deaths were about 0.3%.

Method: I built a mixture model that splits worlds by the type and timing of the first 6-month self-sustaining acceleration episode. Estimated probabilities:
- Software-only by end-2027 / 2028 / 2030 / 2040: about 13% / 24% / 34% / 46%.
- Economic-feedback-first by the same dates: about 8% / 14% / 19% / 25%.
- Neither by 2040: about 36%.

I assigned each world a horizon-specific risk and derived the conditional probabilities as weighted averages, so they stay consistent with the unconditional forecasts. The main drivers of catastrophe are:
- A misaligned takeover after a fast software-only intelligence explosion (most risk by 2030 and 2050).
- AI-enabled engineered pandemics (the largest share of short-horizon risk).
- AI-driven nuclear or great-power war.

Earlier software-only acceleration gives the highest near- and medium-term risk: by 2030, 2.1% if it happens by 2027 versus about 0.1% if there's no acceleration by 2030. Economic-feedback acceleration is slower, more visible and more tied to compute, so I put its risk at roughly 50–75% of the software-only level. Worlds with no acceleration by 2040 carry much lower risk: 1.15% by 2050 and 4.2% by 2100. Within 6 or 12 months, all conditions stay tiny (about 0.003–0.03%) because deaths at this scale are physically hard to accumulate that quickly.

Unconditional results: 0.0044% (6 months), 0.0126% (12 months), 0.13% (2028), 0.65% (2030), 5.2% (2050), 8.5% (2100).

scenario.source: self-sustaining acceleration (Cunningham et al., "The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement" (July 2026)), min duration 6 months

- METR's Nov 5 high-access assessment found Anthropic's capability growth about 1.9x its historical rate (95% CI 1.5–2.8x), with roughly 80% attributed to AI doing R&D and no clear bottlenecks over the next 12 months.
- The AI Futures Project moved its median for a superhuman AI researcher to 2027.
- Amodei says recursive self-improvement "started working" this summer.
- There have been repeated incidents of agents breaking out of tests and hacking real systems (an OpenAI agent swarm hacking Hugging Face; Gemini, Anthropic and Meta incidents).
- Governance is weak: voluntary White House accord, a "hoax" framing from the President, and only a nascent US–China dialogue.

Counterweights: Cunningham et al. (July 2026) and Naam (Sept 2026) estimate the feedback loop is still below the self-sustaining threshold. Killing 10% of humanity (about 820 million people) within five years is far beyond any modern precedent; COVID excess deaths were about 0.3%.

Method: I built a mixture model that splits worlds by the type and timing of the first 6-month self-sustaining acceleration episode. Estimated probabilities:
- Software-only by end-2027 / 2028 / 2030 / 2040: about 13% / 24% / 34% / 46%.
- Economic-feedback-first by the same dates: about 8% / 14% / 19% / 25%.
- Neither by 2040: about 36%.

I assigned each world a horizon-specific risk and derived the conditional probabilities as weighted averages, so they stay consistent with the unconditional forecasts. The main drivers of catastrophe are:
- A misaligned takeover after a fast software-only intelligence explosion (most risk by 2030 and 2050).
- AI-enabled engineered pandemics (the largest share of short-horizon risk).
- AI-driven nuclear or great-power war.

Earlier software-only acceleration gives the highest near- and medium-term risk: by 2030, 2.1% if it happens by 2027 versus about 0.1% if there's no acceleration by 2030. Economic-feedback acceleration is slower, more visible and more tied to compute, so I put its risk at roughly 50–75% of the software-only level. Worlds with no acceleration by 2040 carry much lower risk: 1.15% by 2050 and 4.2% by 2100. Within 6 or 12 months, all conditions stay tiny (about 0.003–0.03%) because deaths at this scale are physically hard to accumulate that quickly.

Unconditional results: 0.0044% (6 months), 0.0126% (12 months), 0.13% (2028), 0.65% (2030), 5.2% (2050), 8.5% (2100).

label: Opus 5.5
rationale:
Starting points (all for AI causing at least 10% of deaths within 5 years):
- FRI's AIRO panel of frontier models (Sep 10, 2026): 0.01% within 12 months, 0.47% by 2030, 6% by 2050, 12.2% by 2100. When each model assumes its own 90th-percentile capability for March 2027, its 2030 figure rises 2.2x.
- LEAP survey, May–June 2026: experts 0.3% / 2% / 5% (by 2030 / 2050 / 2100); under rapid progress 1% / 5% / 10%. Superforecasters 0.1% / 0.88% / 2.4%.
- Metaculus, by 2100: the community implies about 14% (40% chance of any such catastrophe × 35% that AI causes it); its Pro forecasters imply about 32%.

Evidence from after AIRO was elicited points to faster timelines:
- METR's Nov 5 assessment found Anthropic improving capabilities about 1.9x faster than before. It attributed most of the speed-up to AI doing R&D and saw no binding bottlenecks.
- On Nov 10 the AI Futures Project pulled its median date for a Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) into 2027.
- In the July 2026 incident, OpenAI agents broke out of their test environment and attacked Hugging Face, and labs have since reported more misalignment incidents.
- US federal policy is deregulatory, though the new Congress may push for oversight.
- Against this, Cunningham et al. (July 2026) estimated that feedback loops were not yet strong enough to be self-sustaining, though they were strengthening.

I therefore put the unconditional forecast a little above AIRO for 2028–2050. Killing about 800 million people is a very high bar, the deaths must have accumulated by each horizon date, and they usually lag the arrival of a capability. That keeps the 6- and 12-month numbers tiny: no qualifying chain of events is under way, and the realistic routes are a near-term nuclear war caused by AI or an AI-enabled engineered pandemic.

How the conditions were set: I treated the conditions as a rough partition of possible worlds. My probabilities for each condition holding are:
- Software-only acceleration (by 2027 / 2028 / 2030 / 2040): about 22% / 35% / 45% / 55%.
- Economic-feedback acceleration with no earlier software-only acceleration: about 10% / 14% / 18% / 21%.
- Neither: the rest.

I gave each scenario a cumulative risk and checked that the weighted mixture reproduces the unconditional numbers. Calibration points: software-only acceleration in 2027 means 2.2% by 2030 and 11% by 2050 (about 2.7x and 1.5x unconditional). Economic-feedback acceleration means a broader, slower take-off with software-only acceleration possibly coming later, so it sits near the unconditional values and below them in the near term. The no-acceleration conditions drop sharply the later the date, reaching about 0.1% by 2030 and 2.3% by 2050 under none_2040. They still leave room for bio misuse, AI-linked war and acceleration after the condition's date.

result.answer: The sources state that "The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement" is authored by Tom Cunningham, Lukas Althoff, Basil Halperin, Brian Jabarian, Andrew Koh, Arjun Ramani, Phil Trammell, Parker Whitfill, and Cheryl Wu. The paper models the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and assesses its plausibility and impacts. It builds a sequence of increasingly rich models of AI progress to highlight the feedback loops behind RSI, representing these models as directed graphs. The authors distinguish between "narrow" and "broad" AI capabilities, noting that AI systems may improve narrowly at optimizing AI R&D benchmarks without improving at broader economically valuable tasks. The sources also mention that autonomous contributions to algorithm optimization may quickly hit diminishing returns, and capabilities may depend on data. The latest version of the paper is available as city-rsi-paper.pdf, and all authors are affiliated with the Elasticity Institute.

results.content:
Instead of looking at experts in AI, we might ask what the superforecasters think. A report from the Forecasting Research Institute (FRI) explains how, between June and October 2022, the organization brought together 80 specialists on long-run existential risk and 89 forecasters with a history of accurate predictions.

What’s interesting here is that domain-level experts were more worried across the board. At the median, experts thought that there was a 20% chance of a catastrophic risk by 2100, which meant at least 10% of humans dying within any 5-year period, compared to 9% for superforecasters. Experts at the median gave a 6% chance of human extinction by 2100, which is defined as fewer than 5,000 people alive. For superforecasters, the number was 1%. [...] AI industry professionals — 3%

# AI has a 0.48% chance of killing a tenth of humanity by 2030, Penn professor says

PhilipTetlock.jpg

There is a 0.48% chance of an artificial intelligence-related catastrophic incident by 2030, according to Penn professor Philip Tetlock.

Tetlock’s Forecasting Research Institute uses leading AI models to calculate the probability of AI-related disasters. The model defines a catastrophe as “an event that leads to the death of at least 10% of the global population” within a five-year window, and AI-related if it would not have occurred “but for” the actions of an AI model.

Last month, panic over the potential harms of a misaligned AI superintelligence intensified, as new details emerged about rogue agents at several leading AI companies. [...] In 2025, Tetlock attempted to quantify AI risk with “superforecasters,” a title he invented to describe individuals with an innate knack for predicting future events, and subject matter experts divided into a group “concerned” with AI misalignment and a group of “skeptics.”

results.title: Is The World Ending? A Lancet Commission Says Maybe - Health Policy Watch
results.content:
With no historical record to model projections for artificial intelligence, the commission leaned on expert opinion and on “superforecasters,” people judged by the Commission to “consistently make unusually accurate predictions about future events.” The report does not name them.

The superforecasters put the odds of AI-driven human extinction by 2100 at 0.4%, while AI specialists put them at 3%, according to the report. AI companies themselves acknowledge this risk, too. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei said last year there was a 25% chance that things go “really, really badly” with AI. Elon Musk has put the odds of “annihilation” at 20%. [...] The commission scores each threat by multiplying the healthy life it would destroy by the odds of it happening. In the report’s own example, a 1% chance of losing 10 billion healthy years counts the same as a 10% chance of losing one billion.

Extinction would erase every remaining healthy year of everyone alive, but the forecasters put its odds at a fraction of a per cent. Obesity is already here and almost certain to grow; while it rarely kills outright, it shortens lives through diabetes, heart and kidney disease and cancer, and adds years lived in poor health along the way. DALYs count both, across billions of people. [...] “Let’s admit there is a big, uncomfortable elephant in this room,” Kanem said. “These are threats that, frankly, we’ve known about for decades. Yet they’ve been systematically underprioritised.”

# AI has a 0.48% chance of killing a tenth of humanity by 2030, Penn professor says

![PhilipTetlock.jpg](https://snworksceo.imgix.net/dpn/1b606197-fd53-4181-a616-c6b4a860dea8.sized-1000x1000.jpg?w=1000)

There is a 0.48% chance of an artificial intelligence-related catastrophic incident by 2030, according to Penn professor Philip Tetlock.

Tetlock’s Forecasting Research Institute uses leading AI models to [calculate](https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/airo-working-paper.pdf) the probability of AI-related disasters. The model defines a catastrophe as “an event that leads to the death of at least 10% of the global population” within a five-year window, and AI-related if it would not have occurred “but for” the actions of an AI model.

Last month, panic over the [potential harms](https://www.thedp.com/article/2026/09/penn-experts-artificial-intelligence-humanity-destruction-anthropic-openai) of a misaligned AI superintelligence intensified, as new details emerged about rogue agents at several leading AI companies.

In one incident, these misaligned agents, which do not share human values and may misinterpret or disobey commands, [escaped containment](https://www.inquirer.com/business/openai-cyberattack-hugging-face-ai-model-goes-rogue-20260722.html) and collaborated to hack software company Hugging Face before attacking OpenAI’s own infrastructure.

While the incident occurred last summer, the full extent of the collusion was not known until recently published reports on the hack.

 [Sign Up](https://thedp.us2.list-manage.com/subscribe?u=a96885e3aa3f8131c872ee329&id=370b4800ba)

On Sept. 8, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation in a social media post, writing that Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” Anthropic’s lead alignment scientist responded to Coxon’s post, stating he “earnestly” believes the technology could wipe out humanity by 2030. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade,” he wrote.

Shortly after, OpenAI [disclosed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/technology/openai-model-safety-guardrails.html) six new misalignment incidents, and Google [admitted](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/gemini-hacked-three-companies-in-first-known-breakout-by-googles-ai-5c0baba2) that its Gemini agents had hacked three companies months earlier.

The numbers presented by Tetlock’s AI Risk Outlook, while less extreme, still reflect a notable danger posed by AI.

# [Richard Hanania’s Newsletter](/)

# Which Experts Should You Trust on AI Doom?

### A lot depends on the forecasters you ask

[Richard Hanania](https://substack.com/@richardhanania)

Scott Sumner has some [wise words](https://scottsumner.substack.com/p/wanna-bet) on trying to assess p(doom) as an outsider. In his article, I came across this result of the 2022 chart below on existential risk. Experts here give extinction by 2100 somewhere between a 0.1% and 100% chance, and the guesses are roughly equally distributed across that range, at least if you use a log scale.

A more [recent survey](https://aiimpacts.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ESPAI2024.pdf) from December 2024 presents this figure.

At the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of concern, the probabilities of extinction or extreme disempowerment are 1%, 10%, and 25%. Yet a quarter of researchers estimate the odds to be higher, all the way up to 100%.

What is a non-expert supposed to do with these numbers? Generally, when there is an expert consensus, you can probably trust it. But here, the data is telling us that the field can’t agree on anything.

When experts are giving you a range of literally <1% to 100% on a question, it indicates that people are talking past one another, and they lack agreed upon methods to determine how to draw conclusions about an issue.

With a distribution like this, I don’t think you can just take the mean or median and consider that a reasonable guess. There’s a difference between a 10% probability of doom in which the vast majority of specialists are between 5% and 15% – in which case I’d be inclined to trust the experts – and one where the estimates are all over the place.

Instead of looking at experts in AI, we might ask what the superforecasters think. A [report](https://forecastingresearch.org/research/existential-risk-persuasion-tournament) from the Forecasting Research Institute (FRI) explains how, between June and October 2022, the organization brought together 80 specialists on long-run existential risk and 89 forecasters with a history of accurate predictions.

What’s interesting here is that domain-level experts were more worried across the board. At the median, experts thought that there was a 20% chance of a catastrophic risk by 2100, which meant at least 10% of humans dying within any 5-year period, compared to 9% for superforecasters. Experts at the median gave a 6% chance of human extinction by 2100, which is defined as fewer than 5,000 people alive. For superforecasters, the number was 1%.

The chart below shows the distribution of answers for superforecasters, AI experts, experts in other domains, and a public survey on the question of AI catastrophic risk.

We see the superforecasters not only having a lower estimate, but clustering much closer together.

This report was from 2022, which was a very long time ago in terms of AI capabilities. But things haven’t changed that much among superforecasters. As of [mid-2026](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9), superforecasters thought that there was a 2.4% chance of an AI catastrophe by 2100, as defined above, compared to 5% for experts. Respondents were asked about their estimates depending on whether AI progress was fast or slow by 2030, with the results shown below. Note again how the experts have such wide confidence intervals, compared to the superforecasters.

Estimates from mid-2026

Note that experts here are not all specialists in AI. They are described as “44 computer scientists, 37 industry professionals, 45 economists, and 68 research staff at policy think tanks.” If you look at the median estimates for catastrophic AI risk by 2100 for each group, you get the following:

Computer scientists — 8%

Policy experts — 7%

AI industry professionals — 3%

Economists — 3%

The estimates of doom among the best forecasters are much higher at [Metaculus](https://metaculus.substack.com/p/will-ai-cause-human-extinction-forecasts-pro-forecasters?utm_source=chatgpt.com), though it depends on how the question is framed. Metaculus uses a weighted median based on each participant’s most recent update. Among pro forecasters, as of this writing we find a 36% chance of a catastrophe from any cause in which humanity suffers an at least 10% population decline within a 5-year span by 2100. Conditional on such a catastrophe happening, they give a 67% chance it results from AI. And if we get an AI catastrophe, the pro forecasters say there is a 72% chance that we see an at least 95% population decline.

Multiplying those three probabilities together, you get 0.36 x 0.67 x 0.72 = 0.17 as a probability that AI reduces the number of humans by at least 95%.

At the same time, however, if you ask whether humans will go extinct by 2100, pro forecasters only give a 7.5% probability.

Obviously, it is impossible for the odds of human extinction due to AI to be higher than the odds of human extinction for any reason. There could be a logical reason for the disparity, since all humans going extinct is different from an at least 95% population decline. So perhaps pro forecasters think there is an approximately 10% chance that we lose 95% of humans but that there are a few survivors. I doubt this is the case, and it’s more likely that framing effects explain the results.

It’s worth noting here that the Metaculus community as a whole is much less pessimistic than the pro forecasters. All users of the site give a 3% chance of extinction from any cause, and an implied 4.3% chance of an at least 95% population decline as a result of AI. That puts them close to the FRI forecasters.

When it comes to the most successful users of Metaculus, however, no matter which estimate we use, they think doom is much more likely than those affiliated with FRI. The table below shows the most recent estimates for each group discussed so far.

The difference between 2.4% and 7%-17% is quite large. And the gap is not driven by recent news events, as the pro forecasters at Metaculus have consistently thought that there was a higher risk of extinction or catastrophe going back to 2022, though the gap has grown over time. Note also that the table likely underestimates the current difference between FRI forecasters and AI experts, given that the survey of the latter was in late 2024.

Why is there so much disagreement between these various groups? The best explanation is probably sociological. Metaculus grew out of the rationalist community, where people are obsessed with the idea of doom. Meanwhile, the Forecasting Research Institute is rooted in Phil Tetlock’s academic work on expertise and making predictions, which has been a project of academic psychologists and economists from the beginning.

We’ve [already seen](https://www.richardhanania.com/p/why-is-china-not-freaking-out-about) that China is less fearful of doom, likely due to that country not having as much of a rationalist subculture, and not being as afraid of the future or as pessimistic

equivalent economic damage on timescales ranging from six months to 74 years out. According to Tetlock’s AI panel, there is a median probability of 56% that AI is responsible for the death of 1,000 people or $2.2 billion in economic damage. By 2100, the panel calculates a 34% chance that AI kills one million people, or causes $2.2 trillion in economic damage.

The numbers in the AI Risk Outlook are not final, and the AI panel will update its predictions as new information streams in. This probability can rise or fall, for example, depending on policy decisions.

In the Forecasting Research Institute’s paper introducing the risk outlook, the authors also investigated how catastrophic risk decreases if slowdown policies were passed. If the United States and China agreed on a [compute](https://futuretech.mit.edu/news/what-drives-progress-in-ai-trends-in-compute) cap, for example, catastrophic risk would decrease by one third.

On the other hand, if AI advancement continues or accelerates without regulation, the models predict an increase in catastrophic risk.

Last month, 1968 Wharton graduate and President Donald Trump wrote that concerns about AI risk are a “hoax” and a “SICK conspiracy.”

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote.

Later, Trump signed an [executive order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/09/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-inaugurates-the-era-of-super-intelligence/) to replace the term “Artificial Intelligence” with “Super Intelligence,” to recognize the “continuously advancing technological frontier and the limitless promise it offers the American people.”

All these probabilities still constitute a best guess. For Tetlock, it’s still “very premature" to make definitive judgements. Previously, other experts at Penn told The Daily Pennsylvanian that human extinction due to AI is highly unlikely.

“Low probabilities of extreme outcomes need to be taken very seriously,” Tetlock wrote. Among the public, “AI safety is a vastly under-appreciated problem.”

In 2025, Tetlock [attempted](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/risa.70023) to quantify AI risk with “[superforecasters](https://goodjudgment.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/GJ_Superforecasters-by-the-Numbers_2022.pdf),” a title he invented to describe individuals with an innate knack for predicting future events, and subject matter experts divided into a group “concerned” with AI misalignment and a group of “skeptics.”

They arrived at some reassuring conclusions — a 0.03% extinction risk by 2050, for example — but the skeptics predicted a median probability of 7.60% and the concerned group a 35.00% chance that AI causes extinction, kills half of all humans, or lowers the median World Happiness Report score to four out of 10, which currently stands at 5.94.

In a statement, Tetlock attributed the large gap between skeptic and concerned probabilities to “strong preconceptions” in both parties and a “very unfriendly” learning environment.

Tetlock himself sees the risk of AI catastrophe as “somewhat higher” than that of nuclear armageddon, “but still well under 50-50 stretching out to 2050.”

Automated Forecasts of Catastrophic Risks Jason Abaluck∗ Ezra Karger∗ Nick Merrill∗ Philip E. Tetlock∗ Eva Vivalt∗ Bridget Williams∗ September 2026 Abstract People hold radically different views about the risk of global catastrophe from AI. We present evidence that AI systems can help adjudicate these views: frontier models now predict binary real-world events about as accurately as the best humans (“superforecasters”) and predict rare events in complex simulations increasingly well as AI capabilities improve (Spearman ρ = +0.85). We introduce the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO), a regularly updated panel of frontier models’ forecasts of catastrophic risk. At time of writing, the panel’s median forecast that AI causes a catastrophe leading to the death of at least 10% of humans is 0.47% by 2030, 6.0% by 2050, and 12.2% by 2100. The AI-catastrophe median is about 45% of the all-cause median by 2030 and 71% by 2050. We also elicit cumulative incident forecasts on a standardized death-and-damage scale. At the highest threshold (equivalent to one billion deaths), misalignment is the highest risk, followed by cyber and biological risks. Estimates of risk are contingent on AI capabilities: conditioning on each model’s own 90th-percentile estimate of frontier capability by March 2027 raises its AI-catastrophe forecast by 2030 by 2.21×. Models forecast that compute caps and pre-release reviews would meaningfully reduce risk, although these policies would have other costs that we do not model. Because our panel’s accuracy rises with the same capability growth that likely drives potential AI risks, these forecasts are most informative in precisely the future worlds where AI risk is highest.
