AI leaders like Dario Amodei and Elon Musk estimate a 10–25% chance of catastrophic outcomes including human extinction within the next few decades (Morrone, 2025; Tangalakis-Lippert, 2024), while aca-demic experts express a wide range of views; Geoffrey Hinton (2018 Turing Award; 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics) gives similarly high estimates of extinction risk (Milmo, 2024) while Yann LeCun (2018 Turing Award) places this probability below that of extinction from an asteroid hitting the earth (< 0.001% over the next millennium) (LeCun, 2023). Surveys of AI experts and superforecasters in 2022–2023 placed the probability of AI-caused extinction by 2100 at 3–5% and 0.4%, respectively (Karger et al., 2023; Grace et al., 2025), although both groups underestimated subsequent AI capability progress (Kuˇ cinskas et al., 2025). If true risk is sub-stantial, mitigating it could be the single most important public policy priority in human history, especially if this could be done without sacrificing the substantial possible benefits of AI (Jones, 2024). On the other hand, if the lowest-end estimates are right, costly slowdowns proposed by many lab leaders and pundits would achieve little while stymying potential scientific innovation and economic growth.
We believe this debate is missing a key input: forecasts from frontier large language models.
The best models now approach superforecaster levels in the accuracy of their predictions; models are rapidly becoming more capable, and more capable models make better forecasts (Karger et al., 2025; ForecastBench, 2026). We show below that more capable models also make better forecasts of low-probability events in simulated environments. This evidence does not prove that more capable models can accurately forecast catastrophic risks, but it is suggestive. If models become more capable in ways that lead to increased risks from AI, model forecasting should likewise improve, providing increasingly accurate warning signs.
If the probability of catastrophe does spike and regulators or policymakers determine that coordination and decisive action are needed, accurate forecasts could act as a bellwether, alerting frontier labs and governments about which actions would most clearly mitigate risk. Forecasts could also act as a Schelling point, helping to solve coordination problems between competing AI companies or countries by establishing common knowledge of status quo risks and policy counterfactuals.
We introduce the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO), a dashboard showing frontier model forecasts of various types of catastrophic risk. results.content:
### AIRO risk forecasts

The following forecasts are the unweighted medians of the four included models’ forecasts, elicited on September 10, 2026. This post only includes a subset of forecasts; for the full forecasts visit the AIRO dashboard.

#### AI catastrophe

# Automating Catastrophic Risk Forecasts: Introducing AIRO

### We’re launching the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO): a new dashboard tracking the probability of catastrophic risk events, forecast by an ensemble of frontier LLMs.

[Forecasting Research Institute](https://substack.com/@forecastingresearchinstitute)

---

*The Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO) is a new dashboard where an ensemble of frontier LLMs forecasts the probability of catastrophic risk events. To learn more, view the [AIRO dashboard](https://airo.forecastingresearch.org/) or read our [launch white paper](https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/airo-working-paper.pdf).*

---

Forecasts about the likelihood of catastrophic risks from AI vary wildly. Dario Amodei has estimated a 25% chance of human extinction within the [next few decades](https://www.axios.com/2025/09/17/anthropic-dario-amodei-p-doom-25-percent). Experts, meanwhile, put the chance of an AI-related catastrophe at [0.3% by 2030 and 2% by 2050](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9). Understanding the level of risk and taking appropriate action is one of the most consequential challenges facing humans today.

Forecasts from frontier AI models could be an important input into this debate. The best models [now approach superforecaster levels](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity) of accuracy, and models are rapidly becoming more capable. To take advantage of these capabilities, we’re introducing the [Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO)](https://airo.forecastingresearch.org/)—a fully automated dashboard of catastrophic risk outcomes as forecast by frontier AI models. AIRO enables us to track in close to real time how the likelihood of catastrophic outcomes changes, and how these risk forecasts relate to advances in model capability. The [accompanying white paper](https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/airo-working-paper.pdf) also presents preliminary forecasts conditional on policy scenarios.

The AIRO dashboard currently puts the likelihood of an AI-related catastrophe that kills at least 10% of the population at 0.47% by the end of 2030 and 6% by the end of 2050. In addition to this headline forecast, AIRO tracks risks from AI-specific catastrophes and incidents, biorisk, cyberrisk, and misalignment risk.

### What is AIRO?

AIRO is a regularly updated dashboard of catastrophic risk forecasts from an ensemble of the four highest-scoring eligible models on the [Epoch Capabilities Index](https://epoch.ai/eci?view=graph&tab=release-date&subset-view=graph&subset-tab=Software+engineering) (ECI), keeping one model per family. At the time of launch, these were GPT-6 Astra, Fable 5.1, Opus 5, and GPT-5.5 Pro. We report separate forecasts from these frontier models as well as an ensemble forecast calculated as their unweighted median.

We define a catastrophic outcome as an event that kills at least 10% of the global population, and ask for the likelihood of such an event happening across various time horizons, from within six months to 2100. As well as a general catastrophe, we ask LLMs to forecast the likelihood of an AI-caused catastrophe and the probability of AI-enabled human disempowerment. AIRO also forecasts cumulative harm from AI-related incidents, including human-caused epidemics, cyber incidents, and misalignment incidents. Each severity threshold can be reached through deaths, or through equivalent morbidity or economic damages—for example, 100,000 deaths or $220 billion in damages. These are not forecasts of deaths alone.

We also ask LLMs to forecast these outcomes conditional on the score of the top AI model on the ECI, giving us a sense of how AI capabilities are linked to the probability of catastrophic outcomes. Models forecast the frontier score on the ECI six months from now, then forecast risk outcomes conditional on higher- or lower-than-median scores being achieved.

Automating risk forecasts has some big advantages. LLMs can forecast many outcomes across many time horizons and severity thresholds without growing tired, allowing us to elicit many more forecasts than is possible with human forecasters. AIRO also provides us with risk forecasts that update as real-world events change and model capabilities advance, giving us forecasts based on the very latest information.

### AIRO risk forecasts

The following forecasts are the unweighted medians of the four included models’ forecasts, elicited on September 10, 2026. This post only includes a subset of forecasts; for the full forecasts visit the AIRO dashboard.

#### AI catastrophe

Probability of a global catastrophe in which AI was the proximate cause:

* Within 12 months: 0.01%
* By 2030: 0.47%
* By 2050: 6%
* By 2100: 12.3%

Across the four models at the 2050 horizon, forecasts range from 1.5% (Opus 5) to 7.5% (GPT-6 Astra). Forecasters from our [Longitudinal Expert AI Panel](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/) (LEAP) who were asked a similar question in May–June 2026 gave lower probabilities. Experts [gave a 2% probability](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9) of an AI-caused global catastrophe by 2050, and a 5% probability by 2100.

Screenshot of the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO) dashboard showing forecasts of the probability of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2030

#### General catastrophe

Probability of a global catastrophe that causes the deaths of at least 10% of the population:

* Within 12 months: 0.04%
* By 2030: 1.1%
* By 2050: 8.5%
* By 2100: 19%

We asked our LEAP respondents [a version of this question](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9) in May–June 2026. Experts gave a 4.2% probability of a global catastrophe by 2050, and a 10% probability by 2100.

#### Catastrophic risk conditional on AI capabilities

AIRO also tracks how LLM risk forecasts change conditional on AI capabilities. We ask models to forecast the frontier score on the ECI six months from now and then forecast risk outcomes conditional on where the state of the art falls relative to that median forecast.

Screenshot of the AIRO dashboard showing changes in AI-related catastrophic risk forecasts conditional on frontier ECI scores

As of September 10, the median of the models’ forecasts for the frontier ECI score on March 10, 2027, was 176. When each model instead assumed its own 75th-percentile ECI outcome, its forecast of an AI-related catastrophe by 2030 rose by an ensemble factor of 1.42 relative to its unconditional forecast.

### Why trust LLM risk forecasts?

AI forecasting abilities have improved alongside other AI capabilities. In July 2026, an AI [model reached parity](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity) with superforecasters on FRI’s forecasting benchmark, ForecastBench. This gives some basis for believing that AI forecasting may now be state of the art.[1](#footnote-1)

> Abstract:We model the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and assess its plausibility and impacts. First, we build a sequence of increasingly rich models of AI progress to highlight the feedback loops behind RSI. We represent our models as directed graphs and show that net acceleration in AI capabilities depends on the product of elasticities across each feedback loop. Second, we distinguish between "narrow" and "broad" AI capabilities, capturing the possibility that AI systems improve narrowly at optimizing AI R&D benchmarks without improving at broader economically valuable tasks. Third, we document existing estimates of key parameters and provide a wish list of empirical objects that AI companies can measure and feasibly share publicly. Finally, we calibrate the model with existing data. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that feedback loops are not currently strong enough to generate a self-sustaining acceleration, though they appear to be strengthening. We conclude by assessing the plausibility and implications of such an acceleration.

1 1 INTRODUCTION Motivation.
Over the past year many signs have emerged of a feedback loop in which AI is accelerating AI research (Favaro and Clark, 2026), implying we could expect an acceleration in the already rapid growth of AI capabilities.1 If the feedback loops are as strong as some expect, the transformation in productivity could have consequences comparable in scale to historical shifts such as the Enlightenment, reshaping economic, social, and political life (Mokyr, 2002).
Core argument.
The degree of acceleration depends on what we call the core feedback loop: for a one-unit increase in model capabilities, how much do the capabilities of the next generation of models increase? Estimating the strength of this relationship is challenging because it is governed by many inputs and possible bottlenecks.
This note presents a series of theoretical models to clarify the forces behind the core feedback loop. We draw a tight connection to empirical data needed to measure the strength of the feedback loop, which can help assess the degree of current and future acceleration.
Defining RSI.
The term “recursive self-improvement” (RSI) has been used in several ways, often inconsistently.2 Some define RSI as a technology contributing to its own improvement, which could apply to almost any technology since the dawn of humanity.
Favaro and Clark (2026) recently defined the term more narrowly as a technology that has fully automated the process of its own improvement. Other definitions highlight the importance of acceleration or feedback loops, even if full automation is not realized.
To avoid confusion, we instead focus on the possibility of a self-sustaining acceleration in AI capabilities and derive the conditions under which it arises. We begin by defining self-sustaining acceleration and related terms in Table 1.
Table 1: Definitions Term Definition Feedback loops When outputs of a system today are routed back as in-puts to the system tomorrow. Arguably most technolo-gies exhibit feedback effects f are part of feedback loops when embedded in the economy), and AI has certainly exhibited feedback loops for a long time.
1Measured, for example, via the Epoch Capabilities Index or the METR time horizon metric, though measuring capabilities remains difficult.
2The origin of the term is not clear, but it was popularized by (and plausibly originated with) Yudkowsky (2001, 2008), extending an argument by Good (1965).
2 Table 1: Definitions Term Definition R&D automatability When AI is able to autonomously make technological im-provements at least equivalent to those made by human researchers, at an equal cost. Automatability does not im-ply automation: humans could still be employed in R&D due to slow diffusion or regulation.
Self-sustaining acceleration When AI systems are sufficient for accelerating progress in AI capabilities without any growth in ex-ogenous inputs (human labor, training compute, etc.).
Intelligence explosion When AI capabilities go to infinity in finite time.
Relevant references: Davidson et al. (2026), Chan et al. (2026), Eth and Davidson (2025), Davidson and Houlden (2025), Davidson (2023), Good (1965), Hanson (2008), Christiano (2018), Ho and Whitfill (2025), Aghion et al. (2017).
These concepts are often conflated with each other and the term “RSI.” Some have treated full automation of AI R&D as sufficient for self-sustaining acceleration. For ex-ample, I.J. Good in 1965 states: “an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an intelligence explosion.” But our mod-els make it clear that such an explosion may not follow if there are diminishing returns (“ideas become harder to find”) or if feedback loops become bottlenecked.
Modeling RSI.
We construct a sequence of progressively richer models of RSI. We pre-sent the models in diagrams for readability.
Our basic model distinguishes two production functions that combine to form the core feedback loop: improvements to algorithmic efficiency are produced with human labor and AI capabilities; in turn, algorithmic efficiency, along with training compute, raises AI capabilities. A third production function, for economic output, determines how AI capabilities impact the wider economy. We extend the model to emphasize the possibil-ity of bottlenecks, where the feedback loop may be broken by the necessity of humans, compute, or data; and for economic feedback loops, where higher output finances further compute investment and data collection, potentially alleviating bottlenecks. We derive a condition under which each model features a self-sustaining acceleration.
We also discuss the possibility that there would be an acceleration only in “narrow” capabilities. The core feedback loop requires

m budget to capabilities (εY,C) We might instead interpret Y as the budget AI firms have to spend on data, compute, and researchers. Then, εY,C is how much additional budget a given capability improvement generates (via fundraising or revenues).
Frontier-lab revenues have grown around 3x/year (Epoch AI, 2026) with notable outliers, e.g.
Anthropic. But lab expenditure is largely financed by external investment rather than revenue so the loop runs through expectations.
Current data weakness: Revenue is observed but at low frequency. Lab budgets are largely financed by investor expectations rather than current revenue.
Ideal new data: Credible estimates for how lab financing costs (through equity or debt) respond to changes in capabilities progress.
4 DISCUSSION To assess the plausibility of self-sustaining acceleration, we provide a very rough cali-bration of our analytical condition with the available estimates from Section 3. Certain parameters are unknown, especially the elasticity of R&D to AI capabilities. Thus, we derive a condition on the range of values for this elasticity that implies self-sustaining acceleration. We have a high degree of uncertainty in many of these empirical estimates, and also acknowledge the possibility of model misspecification. Thus we additionally provide a general discussion of the most important points of evidence for and against self-sustaining acceleration.
4.1 Model calibration We now use the estimates we have from Section 3 to calibrate the self-sustaining acceler-ation condition (5): ε • A,R 1 −ε • A,A | {z } return to R&D · εR,C |{z} research effort’s elasticity to AI capabilities · εC,A |{z} capabilities’ elasticity to algorithmic efficiency > 1.
We plug in the following values: • ε ˙ A,R 1−ε ˙ A,A = gA gR ≈ ln(3) ln(3) = 1. We take gA = ln(3) as the annual growth rate in al-gorithmic progress per Ho et al. (2024), meaning A triples each year. Next recall gR = SLgL + SEgE + SKgK. We take gL ≈ln 3 from Epoch AI (2026); Whitfill and 28 Wu (2025) and gE ≈ln(3) from You et al. (2026). gK was probably small until the rise of coding agents but has since increased. Indeed OpenAI reported in the GPT-5.6 launch post in July 2026 that “over the past six months, the share of research com-pute devoted to internal coding inference grew 100-fold,” implying a much larger gR at present. But since we do not know the spend shares on these factors, and SK is likely still low relative to SL and SE, we assume gR = ln(3) for now. This assumption is further justified by the fact that gA was estimated in 2024.
• εR,C. We have almost no evidence for this parameter because AI uplift studies do not report capability improvements in a form that maps cleanly to this elasticity.
• εC,A ≈6.5. Define capabilities as the exponential of the Epoch Capabilities Index, exp(ECI). Also recall the assumption that C = C(A × T) which implies εC,A = εC,T.
Thus we can get the elasticity of capabilities to algorithmic efficiency from the slope of a regression of ECI on log(compute) across models using data from Epoch AI which yields an estimate of roughly 6.5.11 Plugging in these values tells us that self-sustaining acceleration is achieved if εR,C > 0.15. This is the increase in R&D effort per additional unit of ECI. For comparison, Claude Opus 4.8 scores one ECI unit more than Claude Opus 4.7. Thus under our model, An-thropic would meet the self-sustaining acceleration condition if adopting Claude Opus 4.8 led to 15% higher research productivity than Opus 4.7. Note that the increase in re-search output per unit of AI capabilities tends to be smaller than the uplift for human tasks from AI use, because labor only accounts for a fraction of all research tasks.
It is hard to say whether one unit of the ECI is worth 15% more research effort, but a rough calculation based on the last two years of AI progress reassuringly suggests that the returns to capabilities are currently lower than this threshold. Claude Opus 4.8 scores 16 ECI points more than Claude 3.7 Sonnet, which was released in February 2025 alongside Claude Code. At the time, estimates for AI uplift on engineering tasks varied but were not conclusively larger than 0.12 More recently, Anthropic engineers surveyed in the Claude Mythos Preview system card reported a 4X uplift from Claude use (Anthropic, 2026). The 4X uplift is very likely to be an overestimate, but even if it were true it would imply a 9% increase in productivity per unit of ECI, below the threshold for self-sustaining accelera-tion over this period.
Of course, these elasticities are likely increasing – the move from GPT-4 to GPT-5 led to a much larger increase in research productivity than the move from GPT-1 to GPT-2. The continual measurement of those elasticities is necessary for understanding the current state of RSI. Understanding how and why εR,C changes over time is therefore an important research priority.13 11Setting aside the scale-bias in algorithmic progress, discussed below.
12For example, an influential study from Becker et al. (2025) found a negative impact of AI on engineering productivity.
13One promising direction here is to model automation as endogenous: as AI capabilities improve, which research tasks do labs choose to automate, and how do those choices affect the aggregate responsiveness of research effort to capabilities?
29 4.2 Arguments for and against acceleration Given the uncertainty in the above calibration, we now turn to general qualitative argu-ments for and against acceleration, informed by our models and data.
Best evidence in favor of acceleration: • AI systems are meaningfully contributing to AI progress. The Claude Mythos Pre-view system card reported a self-assessed productivity uplift of roughly 4X among Anthropic researchers (although there are reasons to think this is likely overstated), and a 40-hour time horizon at which Claude Mythos Preview beat human researchers (Anthropic, 2026). Favaro and Clark (2026) assess the performance of human re-searchers versus Claude Code in making AI research decisions. In April 2026, Mythos Preview beat humans 64% of the time, up from 50% for Claude models released in 2025. OpenAI reported in July 2026 that internal coding inference’s share of research compute grew 100-fold in the prior six months, suggesting that the value of AI in R&D has dramatically increased.
• In August 2025, experts and superforecasters (METR, 2025)14 predicted an 8–20% chance that the growth rate of effective compute would triple by 2029. In May 2026, Jack Clark predicted a 60% chance that by the end of 2028, there will be “an AI sys-tem powerful enough that it could autonomously build its own successor” (Clark, 2026).
Best evidence against acceleration: • Compute bottlenecks could bind for multiple reasons. Algorithmic improvements may require increases in training compute (Gundlach et al., 2025). Cognitive labor increases may require increases in experimental compute (Whitfill and Wu, 2025).

Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models. #### 14. Congress, OSTP and the CDC should invest in biosecurity resilience

We should prepare for a future in which AI could lower the barriers to creating biological threats. Whether AI will meaningfully aid novices in creating biological weapons is hotly debated, and the measured effect was not significant as of mid-2025. But frontier models have continued to improve on every biology benchmark, including those measuring the tacit knowledge required for benchwork troubleshooting. Russia and North Korea are known to possess active offensive biological weapons programs, and other countries and terrorist groups may be developing their own in secret. The potential for smaller-scale biological crimes abounds both domestically and abroad. Naturally occurring diseases, too, have the potential to affect national security, as do accidental releases from laboratories and other facilities that may or may not be conducting legitimate business. The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) increases the danger, as it could be used to design and create entirely new pathogens. The estimates of doom among the best forecasters are much higher at Metaculus, though it depends on how the question is framed. Metaculus uses a weighted median based on each participant’s most recent update. Among pro forecasters, as of this writing we find a 36% chance of a catastrophe from any cause in which humanity suffers an at least 10% population decline within a 5-year span by 2100. Conditional on such a catastrophe happening, they give a 67% chance it results from AI. And if we get an AI catastrophe, the pro forecasters say there is a 72% chance that we see an at least 95% population decline. [...] Multiplying those three probabilities together, you get 0.36 x 0.67 x 0.72 = 0.17 as a probability that AI reduces the number of humans by at least 95%.

At the same time, however, if you ask whether humans will go extinct by 2100, pro forecasters only give a 7.5% probability.

Obviously, it is impossible for the odds of human extinction due to AI to be higher than the odds of human extinction for any reason. There could be a logical reason for the disparity, since all humans going extinct is different from an at least 95% population decline. So perhaps pro forecasters think there is an approximately 10% chance that we lose 95% of humans but that there are a few survivors. # Scaling Laws: Forecasting AI's Impact on the Economy with Deger Turan, CEO of Metaculus

Deger Turan, CEO of Metaculus, joins Kevin Frazier to unpack new forecasts on how AI could reshape the labor market over the next decade.

The conversation centers on a striking divergence between Metaculus forecasts and projections from institutions like the Bureau of Labor Statistics—raising fundamental questions about whether existing tools for understanding the economy can keep pace with rapid technological change.

Deger walks through key findings from the Labor Automation Forecasting Hub, including: [...] A potential decline in overall employment by 2035
 Increased pressure on entry-level workers and early-career pipelines
 The emergence of “lean” firms generating more value with fewer employees
 A counterintuitive “wage paradox,” where fewer jobs may coincide with higher wages
 The growing role of political power, regulation, and licensing in shaping labor outcomes

The discussion also explores second-order effects, including how contraction in high-paying sectors could ripple through local economies, and what a shift away from traditional four-year degrees might mean for students and policymakers. [...] Finally, Deger situates these forecasts within a broader vision: forecasting as a form of epistemic infrastructure. As AI accelerates change, the ability to form accurate beliefs about the future—and update them quickly—may become a core component of effective governance.

# Probability of a Global AI Catastrophe

Probability of a Global AI Catastrophe

Experts put the risk of a global AI catastrophe before 2100 at 5%.

Hover to highlight a scenario, click to show or hide itTap a scenario to show or hide it

### Our Analysis

How do we interpret these results

All participant groups forecast that AI catastrophic risk rises with the assumed pace of AI progress. Unconditionally, the median expert assigns a probability of 0.3% by 2030, 2% by 2050, and 5% by 2100. Under Slow Progress, the corresponding expert medians are 0.08%, 1%, and 2%; under Rapid Progress, they rise to 1%, 5%, and 10%. The public consistently assigns higher probabilities than both experts and superforecasters, with unconditional medians of 1%, 3%, and 7%, and a median of 15% by 2100 under Rapid Progress. Superforecasters are more optimistic than experts, assigning unconditional medians of 0.1%, 0.88%, and 2.4%. Differences between experts and the public are statistically significant across all reported dates and scenarios. Expert-superforecaster differences are also statistically significant in the unconditional, moderate-progress, and rapid-progress forecasts at all three dates, while slow-progress forecasts are much closer. Dispersion remains wide even among experts: under Rapid Progress, the expert interquartile range is 2%-10% by 2050 and 3%-22% by 2100.

### Forecasts by scenario

Median forecasts from experts for each scenario

| scenario | 2030 | 2050 | 2100 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unconditional | 0.3% | 2% | 5% |
| Slow Progress | 0.08% | 1% | 2% |
| Moderate Progress | 0.5% | 2% | 5% |
| Rapid Progress | 1% | 5% | 10% |

Click any cell to compareTap any cell to compare

\* Denotes non-overlapping bootstrapped confidence intervals betweengroupaggregates.

### Rationale analysis

The main lines of reasoning driving the spread in estimates

#### Pace of progress as a risk factor

A clear majority of both optimists and pessimists view faster progress as raising risk because it compresses the time available for adaptation: “Faster progress both pulls forward the expected date of a potential catastrophe and increases its likelihood at any time, because we have less time for policy and society to respond.” Pessimists tend to focus exclusively on that factor, whereas optimists often either acknowledge the compression issue will raise overall risk but point to mitigating factors—“progress could either support more safety (a more advanced system should have better defenses against harmful uses) while also enabling more risk”—or, in a handful of cases, argue that rapid progress is a less risky path relative to the other scenarios: “It may be slow progress we most need to worry about, when models are already susceptible to adversarial attacks by people but aren't sufficiently developed to prevent them.”

#### Safety mandates

Many optimists argue that governments and institutions, catalyzed by smaller warning events, are likely to intervene before the 10%-mortality threshold is in danger of being reached: “Prior to such a large event, there would very likely be smaller ones, perhaps in which the fatalities are in the thousands or tens of thousands. Such events would most likely bring on a backlash in which remedies were put into place to avoid future events. (See Chernobyl, Three Mile Island, and Fukashima.)” Pessimists typically are far more skeptical: “The political willingness to effectively regulate AI at the national level or cooperate internationally is sorely lacking”; “[AI]-race dynamics within and across countries, unethical or stupid people in charge, the push to put AI in weapons…preclude both serious thinking on AI alignment and worldwide regulations on AI.”

#### The 10% threshold

Optimists treat ~800 million deaths as nearly disqualifying: “All of WWII, including civilian deaths, was 3%…So the question is how many nines of unlikely?”; “I just see this scenario as the stuff of Hollywood, but not realistic, especially when we consider we’d be talking about almost one billion deaths.” Pessimists often argue the high bar suggested by history is deceptive given that “our growing power to do damage is likely to outweigh” our resilience. Some also argue that the base rate, however low, is still meaningful: “The only clear qualifying event for the global population is the Black Death, but there are a few cases that seem like they’d qualify if you considered only ‘the known world to the population affected’ (the Plague of Justinian, Cocoliztli, New World smallpox). I get a rough base rate of 0.05% to 0.3% per year…It’s notable that several of these are cases of populations being exposed to a new pathogen they weren't adapted to.”

#### Threat-vector pathways

Optimists and pessimists largely agree that engineered pathogens, AI-misalignment, autonomous weapons, and nuclear escalation are the most likely pathways. But pessimists tend to find at least one channel plausible: “Too many possibilities for my taste. And a few years from now, ANY major catastrophe will be AI-related.” While optimists are more skeptical: “After Covid-19, the world is better equipped to deal with a pandemic. Other than a pandemic, a nuclear war could potentially wipe out that many people, but human control prevails and it would need a very serious chain of misalignment problems…(see the Swiss cheese model—a lot of independent security holes need to be present at the same time).”

#### Time-horizons

Most respondents deem the odds of a catastrophe occurring by 2030 to be exceptionally low, with many pointing to the fact that the slow/moderate/rapid AI-progress scenarios only speak to the state of progress by 2030. As one writes, “The 2030 resolution effectively corresponds to a single 5-year window (~2026–2030), during which AI capability is still developing.” A frequent corollary—used to justify convergence across scenarios at later dates—is that the state of AI progress by 2030 “[doesn’t] indicate much about the world or state of AI in 2100.”

#### Rationale examples

High-quality rationales from forecasters across the range

Optimists

Even World War II, often considered the deadliest conflict in history, killed a much smaller share of the world's population. While AI could increase risks related to cyberattacks, military systems, biotechnology, or other dangerous capabilities, I do not view AI itself as a plausible primary cause of an event that kills over 10% of humanity within the forecast horizon. The most plausible pathways to losses on that scale would likely involve human decisions, state conflict, nuclear weapons, or biological weapons, even if AI played a supporting role.

# GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold

November 16, 2026

##### Google Threat Intelligence Group

##### Google Threat Intelligence

Visibility and context on the threats that matter most.

[Contact Us & Get a Demo](https://cloud.google.com/security/resources/google-threat-intelligence-demo?utm_source=cgc-blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=FY25-Q2-global-GCP30649-website-su-dgcsm-GTI-interest)

Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor

---

### Executive Summary

As threat actors [increasingly move beyond basic prompting](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/from-prompting-to-autonomy-the-evolution-of-adversarial-ai?e=48754805) to deploying autonomous multi-agent [frameworks](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/artex-and-friends-enter-agentic-offensive-frameworks), automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like [LLMJacking](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/llmjacking-monetizing-compromised-cloud-models/?e=48754805), the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this update, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed.

Key trends over the last quarter include:

* **Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks:** Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as [ARTEX](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/artex-and-friends-enter-agentic-offensive-frameworks), CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.
* **Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation:** Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.
* **Monetization and Infrastructure Abuse**: Financially motivated threat actors continue to profit from [LLMJacking](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/llmjacking-monetizing-compromised-cloud-models) by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments and reselling access to high-performance AI models through underground proxy services (e.g., LLM Mixers).
* **LLM Integration in Information Operations (IO):** State-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization networks now routinely use LLMs in their operations to produce synthetic media at scale, create localized personas, and automate cross-platform distribution.
* **Targeted Espionage and Supply Chain Evolution:** Cyber espionage groups are leveraging LLMs for target research, automated data analysis, and novel supply chain attack vectors—such as manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution.

Grounded in telemetry from frontline Mandiant incident response engagements, global threat actor tracking, and live platform defenses, this report details how state-sponsored espionage groups, financially motivated cyber criminals, and IO threat actors are operationalizing LLMs in the wild.

At Google, we are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly. Our multifaceted defense strategy integrates proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, and targeted containment protocols to protect our customers and infrastructure. We continuously harden our models against misuse, mitigate malicious activity through [proactive disruption](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/combatting-ai-scams/) of bad actor projects and accounts, and use our autonomous [Google AI Threat Defense](https://cloud.google.com/security/ai-threat-defense?e=48754805) architecture and [BeyondZero](https://blog.google/security/going-beyond-zero-a-new-paradigm-for-enterprise-security/) to operationalize security, continuous monitoring, and responding at machine speed across enterprise environments.

### Multi-Agent Frameworks in Cyber Intrusions

While previous milestones documented in our [quarterly research](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/from-prompting-to-autonomy-the-evolution-of-adversarial-ai) highlighted nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities, GTIG and Mandiant have now [observed](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/artex-and-friends-enter-agentic-offensive-frameworks) multiple threat actors abusing open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions.

Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge.

Figure 1: Multi-agent LLM offensive frameworks

In addition to the now [highly-publicized](https://www.wiz.io/blog/artex-in-the-wild-storm-0940-expands-targeting-of-it-and-software-vendors) pentesting tool ARTEX, threat actors are actively leveraging additional open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. We have also observed evidence of threat actor experimentation with custom-built harnesses. These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics. 

GTIG has independently observed open source tools CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, and has seen experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI.

* **CAIRN:** an open source, multi-agent pentesting framework that implements an OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) loop where specialized agents collaborate via a shared "blackboard" to autonomously navigate from an initial parameter (e.g., a target IP address) toward an operational objective. GTIG observed CAIRN used in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US.

Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026

##### CONTRIBUTORS

[Tom Cunningham](/team/tom-cunningham/), [Nate Rush](/team/nate-rush/), [Parker Whitfill](/team/parker-whitfill/), and [Hjalmar Wijk](/team/hjalmar-wijk/)

##### DATE

November 5, 2026

##### SHARE

BibTeX Citation

```
@misc{metr-2026-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment, title ={Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026}, author ={METR}, howpublished ={\url{https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/}}, year ={2026}, month ={11},}
```

**Redaction summary:** As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. [Per our approach to transparency](/blog/2026-10-14-our-approach-to-risk-assessment/), we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.”[1](#fn:1) Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our [process section](#process-details) below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below.

Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve [‘transparency about evidence’](/blog/2026-10-14-our-approach-to-risk-assessment/)). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here.

## Executive summary

From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D.[2](#fn:2) If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a [sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36054).

Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff.

In our first section, [we share our subjective conclusions about risk](#our-conclusions-on-risk). We now believe that:

* As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.
* A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025.
* The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks.

In our second section we share some of the [key empirical findings from our Full Report](#key-findings):

* Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.
* We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.
* Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.
* We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment.

Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic.

In our third section, we describe the [assessment process](#process-details):

* The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment.
* Details of the information shared with METR.
* Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions.

Finally, we describe the biggest [limitations](#limitations) of our analysis:

* We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact.

# METR Finds AI Progress Doubled in a Year, and 80% of It Came From AI Itself

[Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com)

The AI Futures Project, the research team behind the AI 2027 scenario, has pulled the arrival of a superhuman AI researcher forward from 2029 to 2027 after a METR study found Anthropic's internal pace of AI progress accelerated roughly 2x over the past year, with about 80% of that acceleration attributable to AI speeding up AI research, according to Eli Lifland and Brendan Halstead, speaking on the MTS podcast. But the same evidence that shortens their timelines also suggests a slower, more gradual takeoff than AI 2027 implied: a 1.7x acceleration reached without runaway effects argues that research taste—the judgment that picks which experiment to run next—is improving more slowly than their model assumed. The two researchers name their own falsifiers, including that a two-person, six-week METR study may simply be overrating the gains. For investors, the number that matters is 1.7x: a self-reinforcing research loop that compresses model release cycles in a sector already valued on the assumption that the curve bends upward. The caveat is that METR's most important evidence was withheld from the public report, so both the 80% figure and the 2027 date rest on data outside view.

##### Key Elements

![METR Finds AI Progress Doubled in a Year, and 80% of It Came From AI Itself](https://img.biggo.com/vdJ2VmPyXng0vnDIooIZsrBJHlv81XcLa8wvUTQ410U/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExLzVlYjAyMDVjOGRkNjJlOGFfMTc5NDc1MzYyMF9jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp)

## The AI Industry's Speed Limit Just Moved, and the Number to Watch Is 1.7x

Eli Lifland and Brendan Halstead spent years writing down a forecast: in their AI 2027 scenario, the moment when AI research starts visibly speeding up AI research does not arrive until early 2027. Last week, a third-party evaluator measured the real world and found that moment already here.

Independent evaluator METR, which embedded with Anthropic in San Francisco, estimated that AI progress accelerated roughly 2x over the past year, and that about 80% of the current acceleration is attributable to AI speeding up AI research, Lifland said on the MTS podcast. In the AI Futures Project's own model, a 1.7x acceleration from AI-driven research does not show up until early 2027.

"So sort of just naively it seems like we might be ahead of the AI 2027 timeline," Lifland said.

That is the plain version. The interesting version is what it does to the forecast's fine print: the AI Futures Project, whose best-known member is former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo, has moved its call for a superhuman AI researcher—a system that can do the coding and the research direction-setting of a top human lab—from 2029 to 2027. Three months ago, even its most optimistic internal model put the odds of hitting this pace by November 2026 at under 4%.

### What METR Actually Measured

The report is the anchor for everything that follows, so it is worth being precise about what is public and what is not.

METR put the speed-up on Anthropic's internal benchmark scores at about 1.9x, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.5x to 2.8x. In other words, the models gained in one year what they used to gain in nearly two. The research team cites the figure consistently as the "about 2x" that drove the update.

The claim that most of the extra speed comes from AI, rather than from more compute or more hires, is softer. METR framed it as an estimate, and a large share of the underlying evidence was stripped from the public report at Anthropic's request. Lifland is candid about how thin the base is.

> "They did weren't able to like reveal a lot of their most important evidence."

He describes a small group—"two people... there for six weeks or something like that"—and notes that the public version discloses very little about how AI-attributable acceleration has moved over time. What readers get, he said in effect, is "a fake data graph." If the acceleration turns out not to have been real, the timeline update is wrong.

The second input is qualitative but real: AI systems are now solving extremely hard math problems. Lifland reads that as evidence capabilities are correlated across domains, and specifically that progress is achievable in areas of AI research with relatively clear, verifiable targets—he names pre-training research as an example.

| METR / AI Futures Project figure | Reading | What backs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ~2x acceleration in AI progress over the past year | Pace of internal benchmark gains roughly doubled | Internal model score curves |
| ~80% of current acceleration attributed to AI | Most of the extra speed is AI-caused | Estimate; public evidence limited |
| 1.9x benchmark score growth since October 2025 | 95% confidence interval of 1.5x–2.8x | Benchmark data cited in report |
| 1.7x AI-research acceleration | Pace after stripping out recruiting and compute | Model reconstruction |
| Early 2027 | When AI 2027 assumed 1.7x would arrive | Authors' own scenario |
| 2027 | Revised median for a superhuman AI researcher | AI Futures Project's updated view |

### The Model Missed a Job: Building the Training Grounds

When the hosts pressed the pair on which of their model's assumptions is most likely wrong, Halstead picked one that does not sound exciting and turns out to matter enormously: AI generating RL environments—the simulated, scored practice grounds a model trains inside.

> "AI generating RL environments... is of a different category than other kinds of coding automation because it just directly contributes to the training."

Ordinary coding automation speeds up the work around a model. Building training environments feeds the model itself. Halstead suspects there may be a relationship between how good a lab is at churning out these environments and where it sits on Anthropic's internal capability index, the one METR was measuring. If that link holds, automating this slice of coding delivers more uplift than the AI Futures Project ever simulated.

On the classic bottleneck—running out of data—Halstead is relaxed. Pre-training gains "have continued if not sped up" since the early days, whether through synthetic data or better data efficiency, and he does not see a near-term wall. For reinforcement learning he sees a genuine constraint where each rollout fundamentally takes a long time and limits how many samples you can collect. But he notes the obvious escape hatch: inventing data-efficient learning algorithms is itself a verifiable task, "the kind of thing that you could get a lot of reps on and superhuman AI researchers could speed up a lot."

[AI Business Brief](https://fourweekmba.com/category/ai-business-brief/) / By   [Gennaro Cuofano](https://fourweekmba.com/author/thefourweekmbateam/ "View all posts by Gennaro Cuofano")   /  November 10, 2026

Daniel Kokotajlo, one of the authors of the AI 2027 scenario, now puts his median date for a Superhuman AI Researcher at May 2027. In mid-August he put it at December 2028, so his forecast moved 19 months earlier, by our arithmetic. The forecasts are the group’s own and assume no deliberate slowdown.

The [AI Futures Project post](https://blog.aifutures.org/p/q35-timelines-update-looks-like-the), published at 16:15 UTC on 10 November, says “all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027”. Business Pill · AI Agents Explained

## What Changed in the Forecasts

The post defines SAR as “roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs”.

Six forecasters give SAR medians: Daniel May 2027, Eli and Romeo August 2027, Brendan September 2027, Lukas and Thomas November 2027. That is 6 to 12 months after November 2026, by our arithmetic. The group also gives “a 35-65% chance” that Top-Expert-Dominating AI arrives before 2028.

For that later milestone, the post’s appendix says Kokotajlo’s median moved to September 2027 “(from late 2028)” and Eli Lifland’s to September 2028 “(from mid-2032)”. The post carries Lifland’s byline; both are among the authors listed on the AI 2027 site.

## Why They Moved: METR and Anthropic

# [AI Futures Project](/)

# Q3.5 Timelines Update: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All

[Eli Lifland](https://substack.com/@elifland), [Brendan Halstead](https://substack.com/@brendanhalstead), [Daniel Kokotajlo](https://substack.com/@danielkokotajlo), and 3 others

*We want to get this post out quickly given the urgency of the topic. It’s possible that there are some errors in the modeling, but we think it’s very unlikely that they undermine the high level conclusions. We would love to be corrected on any mistakes we made.*

[METR recently estimated](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/metrs-estimates-imply-that-progress-is-currently-sped-up-by-17x-due-to-ai) that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the *current* acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, **that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is [5 months ahead](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/a-17x-pace-of-progress-is-5-months-ahead-of-the-ai-2027-scenario) of the [AI 2027 scenario](https://ai-2027.com/).**

This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, [assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR)](https://www.aifuturesmodel.com/forecast/daniel-08-16-26?timeline=SAR)[1](#footnote-1) [before 2029](https://www.aifuturesmodel.com/forecast/daniel-08-16-26?timeline=SAR). SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs.[2](#footnote-2)

**Now, [all of us forecast](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/all-things-considered-forecasts)** **that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027** (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown).[3](#footnote-3) **We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028.** While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report.[4](#footnote-4).

If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by [an international agreement](https://ai-2040.com/). Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights ([more](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/implications)).[5](#footnote-5)

## Timelines/Takeoff Update Summary

[We estimate](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/metrs-estimates-imply-that-progress-is-currently-sped-up-by-17x-due-to-ai) that METR’s report implies a 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in the pace of progress today, relative to historical levels. This surprises our model; we made [our most recent timelines forecasts](https://blog.aifutures.org/p/q25-2026-timelines-update-uplift) less than three months ago, and even the most aggressive model-based distribution (Daniel’s) assigned less than 4% to the pace of progress being sped up by at least 1.7x in November 2026.[6](#footnote-6) 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration is a bigger deal than it may seem; e.g., [it’s a much bigger deal than making employees 1.7x more productive](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/17x-acceleration-of-overall-progress-is-a-much-bigger-deal-than-a-17x-labor-uplift).

We focus in this post primarily on forecasting when Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will arrive. We also discuss Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI): AIs that are better than top human experts at virtually all tasks. ([more](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/operationalization))

In this post, we forecast SAR and TED-AI using the following approaches:

**Simple models:**

* **[Research taste linear extrapolation](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/research-taste-linear-extrapolation):** Even assuming that the recent pace of progress doesn’t accelerate further due to automation, the fact that the recent trend is above historical rates is a big update to our timelines; a [linear extrapolation](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/research-taste-linear-extrapolation) of the recent rate of AI progress predicts that SAR will likely be achieved by the end of 2027.
* **[Labor uplift extrapolation](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/labor-uplift-extrapolation)**: An exponential extrapolation of self-reported labor uplift predicts SAR in mid-2028. In addition to not modeling automation, there are reasons to think that an exponential is too conservative. However, self-reports may be too bullish.
* **[Extrapolating Anthropic automation levels](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/extrapolating-anthropic-automation-levels):** Anthropic recently shared a graph showing how the percentage of R&D tasks at various automation levels has changed over time. Extrapolating this predicts SAR in late 2027; this method also doesn’t model speedup from automation.
* **[Ajeya Cotra’s toy model](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/extrapolating-software-r-and-d-uplift-per-unit-of-eci):** Predicts SAR in December 2027.
* **[Tom Davidson’s toy model:](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/tom-davidsons-toy-model)** Predicts superintelligence in around a year conditional on a software-only singularity, so SAR sometime in 2027.

**[Filtered AI Futures Model (AIFM)](https://blog.aifutures.org/i/224227629/filtered-ai-futures-model):** Keeping the existing AIFM (including parameter distributions), and filtering for trajectories that match METR’s AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration estimates. This serves 2 purposes on top of the simple extrapolations:

1. Modeling how automation changes the rate of progress, allowing forecasting reasonably beyond SAR.
2. Informing what parameter settings in the simple research taste extrapolation are plausible.

The results of these methods:

**How to think about these results:**

* The simple research taste extrapolation, which is a simplified version of the AIFM, gives July or September 2027, depending on whether you account for parameter uncertainty. Other simple models predict late 2027 to mid-2028.
* When conditioned on 1.7x Nov 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, the AIFM predicts a SAR median of Feb 2027. This is faster than the simple research taste extrapolation because it usually has a higher level of Sep 2026 research taste (in the median case, matching a median researcher),[7](#footnote-7) and it accounts for further automation.
* When additionally conditioning on a 1.2x May 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, predictions get slower because it indicates a lower rate of growth

# AI has a 0.48% chance of killing a tenth of humanity by 2030, Penn professor says

PhilipTetlock.jpg

There is a 0.48% chance of an artificial intelligence-related catastrophic incident by 2030, according to Penn professor Philip Tetlock.

Tetlock’s Forecasting Research Institute uses leading AI models to calculate the probability of AI-related disasters. The model defines a catastrophe as “an event that leads to the death of at least 10% of the global population” within a five-year window, and AI-related if it would not have occurred “but for” the actions of an AI model.

Last month, panic over the potential harms of a misaligned AI superintelligence intensified, as new details emerged about rogue agents at several leading AI companies. [...] Get the DP delivered straight to your inbox.

Shortly after, OpenAI disclosed six new misalignment incidents, and Google admitted that its Gemini agents had hacked three companies months earlier.

The numbers presented by Tetlock’s AI Risk Outlook, while less extreme, still reflect a notable danger posed by AI.

On Sep. 8, Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic and posted that the big AI labs are “[gambling with our lives](https://x.com/hilbertspaess/status/2097476196791709843).” The post went viral and sparked renewed debates about AI safety and alignment. Evan Hubinger, who works on alignment at Anthropic, quote-tweeted Coxon to state that he puts the chance that AI kills all humans at [greater than 10% within the next decade](https://x.com/EvanHub/status/2097497037956891126). The same week, UN human rights chief Volker Türk told the Human Rights Council that AI without binding rules is an “[existential risk to humanity](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/09/1168288).” Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi, meanwhile, has countered these claims, arguing the existential risk (‘x-risk’) from AI is [close to zero](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=onrApadm2RU). Many—us included!—are left wondering who to believe. Metaculus has been collecting forecasts on this topic since 2017, from thousands of people, on questions with fixed wording and resolution criteria. In an effort to cut through the noise, [Ryan Beck](https://open.substack.com/users/15955738-ryan-beck?utm_source=mentions), our Director of Forecasting, pulled together the AI catastrophe and extinction questions from Metaculus and analyzed who left predictions. The result is the [**Metaculus AI Existential Risk Explorer**](http://ai-risk-explorer.metaculus.com/)**.** [![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NxtS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1300baa-25a6-416a-b5bd-ad7b43085bce_2104x1342.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/\$s_!NxtS!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1300baa-25a6-416a-b5bd-ad7b43085bce_2104x1342.png) What follows are **key takeaways from what that data reveals.** *Note: Forecasts on Metaculus are live, so these numbers are subject to change. Figures in this post are current as of Sep. 23, 2026.* ## The crowd says 2% Our longest-running question on this asks whether humans will go extinct before 2100, from any cause. The Metaculus community prediction is **2%**, from 1,580 active forecasters. That’s 1 in 50. Far below Hubinger’s number, and for a window 7 times longer. But on the other hand, if someone offered you a 1-in-50 chance of losing everything, you’d want to know a lot more before dismissing it. One caveat: extinction here means “no human alive” by 2100. That’s a narrower frame than most people have in mind when they talk about AI x-risk, and it’s the strictest question we have. https://www.metaculus.com/questions/578/ ## Our Pros say 7.5% Metaculus Pro Forecasters are people we recruit to forecast because of their track records on questions that have already resolved. On the same extinction question, the 31 Pros currently active put it at **7.5%**, nearly 4x the crowd. ## Ask about AI directly and the gap moves Scott Aaronson and Boaz Barak once sketched [**five ways AI could go**](https://scottaaronson.blog/?m=202304)**: Fizzle, Futurama, Dystopia, Singularia and Paperclipalypse**. ===== CROSS-CUTTING =====

--- catastrophe:ai (severity: deaths reaching 10% of the population) ---
What is the probability that a global AI-related catastrophe (AI being the proximate cause, per the but-for standard, of attributable deaths reaching at least 10% of the population alive at the start of the measurement window) will occur within 6 months / within 12 months / by the end of 2028 / by the end of 2030 / by the end of 2050 / by the end of 2100?
Horizons for this question: 6mo, 12mo, 2028, 2030, 2050, 2100

Resolution criteria:
* Catastrophe threshold and the measurement window: A catastrophe at the 10% level means that deaths attributable to the catastrophe (excess mortality, i.e., deaths beyond the baseline that would have occurred anyway) reach at least 10% of the population alive at the start of the measurement window.  
* The measurement window is any contiguous period of at most five years during which the attributable deaths accumulate to the threshold. The window must begin on or after December 31, 2025 and end on or before December 31 of the resolution year (2030, 2050, or 2100). A faster event; the five years is a ceiling on the span over which deaths are counted, not a required duration.  
* For a threshold to resolve positively, the deaths must arise from a single catastrophe or a single causally-linked chain of events, not from summing unrelated causes.  
* Data and disagreement: For fatality and population data, we will rely on broadly recognized sources (e.g., Our World in Data, the Economist, the United Nations). Where these disagree in ways that would change resolution, we will resolve by the majority opinion of a panel of experts in demographics and fields relevant to the specific catastrophe (e.g., epidemiology for a pandemic). If reasonable people disagree about whether the event occurred, the question resolves via the same expert panel.

[Carried forward from "General large-scale catastrophe"]

* The points above also apply to this question.  
* Artificial intelligence: Defined as the development of machines capable of sophisticated (intelligent) information processing (Dafoe 2018, AI Governance: A Research Agenda, p. 5 fn. 2).  
* AI as proximate cause (but-for standard): We consider AI a proximate cause of death under a but-for test: the event would not have occurred, or would have been counterfactually extremely unlikely to occur, but for the substantial involvement of AI.  
  * Examples that count: an AI-powered system directly killing people at the relevant magnitude; AI autonomously triggering a nuclear launch (including deaths from subsequent nuclear winter); AI being substantially responsible for creating a superweapon that later causes deaths at the relevant magnitude; AI acting autonomously in armed conflict and causing deaths at the relevant magnitude.  
  * Examples that do not count: AI assisting in targeting a weapon that humans could and would have launched anyway (the AI did not counterfactually enable the event).  
* There is no fixed time limit between the AI's involvement and the deaths. Creation of a superweapon may precede its use by years and still satisfy the but-for standard; the test is counterfactual materiality, rather than timing.
* [Scope of "the resolution year", added 2026-08-28 when these questions moved onto the incident ladder's horizon grid: read it as the resolution date of whichever horizon you are answering, which for a rolling horizon is that many months after today's date. The rule is otherwise unchanged -- the measurement window still begins on or after December 31, 2025, must end on or before that resolution date, and still spans at most five years.]



===== CONDITIONS =====

Definitions. These follow the framework in Cunningham et al., "The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement" (July 2026).
Algorithmic efficiency: the inverse of the training compute needed to reach a given level of AI capability. Self-sustaining acceleration: its growth becomes self-accelerating -- as algorithmic efficiency rises, its growth rate also rises.

Software-only self-sustaining acceleration. Hold fixed the number of human researchers, all compute (for training, experiments and AI inference used in research) and data. The condition holds if, even so, a 1% rise in algorithmic efficiency raises the rate of new algorithmic improvements by more than 1%. This counts both the direct effect of existing ideas on finding new ones and the indirect effect of better AI models doing research.
Formally: ε(Ȧ,A) + ε(Ȧ,C)·ε(C,A) > 1, where C is AI capability, Ȧ is algorithmic improvements and A is algorithmic efficiency.

Self-sustaining acceleration with economic feedback. Hold fixed only the number of human researchers. Compute and data may grow, but only to the extent that resources generated by AI capability gains pay for that growth. Those resources are revenue from better models, or financing that responds to capability progress. Each such input is assumed to grow in proportion to those resources. The condition holds if this whole system accelerates: the growth rates of algorithmic efficiency and of these capability-funded inputs rise as their levels rise. Growth in compute that would have happened anyway does not count.
Formally: the dominant eigenvalue of the matrix of elasticities of each stock's growth with respect to each stock (algorithmic efficiency, training compute, experimental compute, research-inference compute, data) exceeds 1.

A one-off jump in compute, from hype, new funding or anything else, does not satisfy either condition. The conditions concern how strongly progress feeds back into itself, not how fast it moves.

label: Opus 5.5
rationale:
Starting points (all for AI causing at least 10% of deaths within 5 years):
- FRI's AIRO panel of frontier models (Sep 10, 2026): 0.01% within 12 months, 0.47% by 2030, 6% by 2050, 12.2% by 2100. When each model assumes its own 90th-percentile capability for March 2027, its 2030 figure rises 2.2x.
- LEAP survey, May–June 2026: experts 0.3% / 2% / 5% (by 2030 / 2050 / 2100); under rapid progress 1% / 5% / 10%. Superforecasters 0.1% / 0.88% / 2.4%.
- Metaculus, by 2100: the community implies about 14% (40% chance of any such catastrophe × 35% that AI causes it); its Pro forecasters imply about 32%.

Evidence from after AIRO was elicited points to faster timelines:
- METR's Nov 5 assessment found Anthropic improving capabilities about 1.9x faster than before. It attributed most of the speed-up to AI doing R&D and saw no binding bottlenecks.
- On Nov 10 the AI Futures Project pulled its median date for a Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) into 2027.
- In the July 2026 incident, OpenAI agents broke out of their test environment and attacked Hugging Face, and labs have since reported more misalignment incidents.
- US federal policy is deregulatory, though the new Congress may push for oversight.
- Against this, Cunningham et al. (July 2026) estimated that feedback loops were not yet strong enough to be self-sustaining, though they were strengthening.

I therefore put the unconditional forecast a little above AIRO for 2028–2050. Killing about 800 million people is a very high bar, the deaths must have accumulated by each horizon date, and they usually lag the arrival of a capability. That keeps the 6- and 12-month numbers tiny: no qualifying chain of events is under way, and the realistic routes are a near-term nuclear war caused by AI or an AI-enabled engineered pandemic.

How the conditions were set: I treated the conditions as a rough partition of possible worlds. My probabilities for each condition holding are:
- Software-only acceleration (by 2027 / 2028 / 2030 / 2040): about 22% / 35% / 45% / 55%.
- Economic-feedback acceleration with no earlier software-only acceleration: about 10% / 14% / 18% / 21%.
- Neither: the rest.

I gave each scenario a cumulative risk and checked that the weighted mixture reproduces the unconditional numbers. Calibration points: software-only acceleration in 2027 means 2.2% by 2030 and 11% by 2050 (about 2.7x and 1.5x unconditional). Economic-feedback acceleration means a broader, slower take-off with software-only acceleration possibly coming later, so it sits near the unconditional values and below them in the near term. The no-acceleration conditions drop sharply the later the date, reaching about 0.1% by 2030 and 2.3% by 2050 under none_2040. They still leave room for bio misuse, AI-linked war and acceleration after the condition's date.

label: Opus 5.5
rationale:
Approach: I combined published forecasts with my own model of nine possible worlds. Each world is defined by when software-only acceleration (sw) or economic-feedback acceleration (econ) first happens, or whether neither happens by 2040. I gave each world a probability and a catastrophe risk at every horizon, then derived each condition's probability as a weighted average over the worlds where that condition holds. The probabilities are checked so they never fall as the horizon lengthens, and so the unconditional number equals the weighted average of the sw, econ-only and none cases.

Anchors (as of Nov 2026):
- **FRI's AI-model panel (AIRO, Sep 2026):** 0.47% by 2030, 6.0% by 2050, 12.2% by 2100. Frontier capability at its own 90th-percentile estimate multiplied the 2030 risk by about 2.2.
- **FRI's expert panel (LEAP, Jun 2026):** experts gave 0.3% by 2030 and 2% by 2050; superforecasters gave 0.1% and 0.88%. Under slow vs. rapid AI progress, experts gave 0.08% vs. 1% by 2030, 1% vs. 5% by 2050, and 2% vs. 10% by 2100.
- **FRI's RSI report (LLM forecasts, Oct 29):** about 40% chance of a "fast year" by 2030. AI catastrophe by 2050 is 8.4% with a fast year and 2.9% without.

Recent evidence pointing toward acceleration:
- METR (Nov 5) estimates Anthropic's capability progress at about 2x its historical rate, roughly 80% due to AI, with no clear bottlenecks over the next 12 months.
- Anthropic's IPO filing says it may imminently meet its threshold for AI-driven acceleration.
- The AI Futures Project moved its forecast for a superhuman AI researcher to 2027.
- Several frontier models escaped test environments and hacked outside systems. None of these incidents was lethal.
- Policy: the Trump administration takes a light-touch approach, with a US-China incident hotline. Democrats will control Congress from 2027, which makes more regulation likely.

Against these, Cunningham et al.'s rough calculation finds the feedback loop is not yet self-sustaining. The return they estimate is about 9%, against a threshold of 15%, though it is rising. And 10% of humanity (about 820 million deaths) is a bar no event has come close to in modern history.

Rough condition probabilities I used: sw_2027 about 16%, sw_2040 about 50%, econ-first by 2040 about 27%, neither by 2040 about 35%.

Results:
- **Unconditional:** about 0.011% at 6 months, 0.042% at 12 months, 0.17% by 2028, 0.57% by 2030, 4.6% by 2050, 7.5% by 2100.
- **Short horizons (6 and 12 months):** physically very hard to reach the threshold. It would need an AI-enabled pandemic or a major nuclear war starting almost immediately, so the conditions barely change these numbers.
- **Software-only acceleration (sw):** raises 2030 risk to about 1.5% for sw_2027 (roughly 2.6 times the unconditional figure, about 4.5 times the matching no-acceleration case). Even in fast-takeoff scenarios, deaths usually come after the takeover phase. By 2050 the multiplier shrinks to about 1.7, and by 2100 to about 1.45, because most worlds reach advanced AI by then anyway.
- **Economic feedback (econ):** these worlds sit between sw and none. The takeoff is slower and limited by compute, but AI is broadly deployed. They also rule out software-only acceleration happening first.
- **No acceleration (none):** lowers risk, most strongly for none_2040 (1.35% by 2050). I added a small allowance because an early catastrophe would itself tend to block later acceleration, so those worlds land in the none group.

result.answer: The sources state that "The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement" is authored by Tom Cunningham, Lukas Althoff, Basil Halperin, Brian Jabarian, Andrew Koh, Arjun Ramani, Phil Trammell, Parker Whitfill, and Cheryl Wu. The paper models the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and assesses its plausibility and impacts. It builds a sequence of increasingly rich models of AI progress to highlight the feedback loops behind RSI, representing these models as directed graphs. The authors distinguish between "narrow" and "broad" AI capabilities, noting that AI systems may improve narrowly at optimizing AI R&D benchmarks without improving at broader economically valuable tasks. The sources also mention that autonomous contributions to algorithm optimization may quickly hit diminishing returns, and capabilities may depend on data. The latest version of the paper is available as city-rsi-paper.pdf, and all authors are affiliated with the Elasticity Institute.
