# METR Finds AI Progress Doubled in a Year, and 80% of It Came From AI Itself

[Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com)

The AI Futures Project, the research team behind the AI 2027 scenario, has pulled the arrival of a superhuman AI researcher forward from 2029 to 2027 after a METR study found Anthropic's internal pace of AI progress accelerated roughly 2x over the past year, with about 80% of that acceleration attributable to AI speeding up AI research, according to Eli Lifland and Brendan Halstead, speaking on the MTS podcast. But the same evidence that shortens their timelines also suggests a slower, more gradual takeoff than AI 2027 implied: a 1.7x acceleration reached without runaway effects argues that research taste—the judgment that picks which experiment to run next—is improving more slowly than their model assumed. The two researchers name their own falsifiers, including that a two-person, six-week METR study may simply be overrating the gains. For investors, the number that matters is 1.7x: a self-reinforcing research loop that compresses model release cycles in a sector already valued on the assumption that the curve bends upward. The caveat is that METR's most important evidence was withheld from the public report, so both the 80% figure and the 2027 date rest on data outside view.

##### Key Elements

![METR Finds AI Progress Doubled in a Year, and 80% of It Came From AI Itself](https://img.biggo.com/vdJ2VmPyXng0vnDIooIZsrBJHlv81XcLa8wvUTQ410U/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExLzVlYjAyMDVjOGRkNjJlOGFfMTc5NDc1MzYyMF9jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp)

## The AI Industry's Speed Limit Just Moved, and the Number to Watch Is 1.7x

Eli Lifland and Brendan Halstead spent years writing down a forecast: in their AI 2027 scenario, the moment when AI research starts visibly speeding up AI research does not arrive until early 2027. Last week, a third-party evaluator measured the real world and found that moment already here.

Independent evaluator METR, which embedded with Anthropic in San Francisco, estimated that AI progress accelerated roughly 2x over the past year, and that about 80% of the current acceleration is attributable to AI speeding up AI research, Lifland said on the MTS podcast. In the AI Futures Project's own model, a 1.7x acceleration from AI-driven research does not show up until early 2027.

"So sort of just naively it seems like we might be ahead of the AI 2027 timeline," Lifland said.

That is the plain version. The interesting version is what it does to the forecast's fine print: the AI Futures Project, whose best-known member is former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo, has moved its call for a superhuman AI researcher—a system that can do the coding and the research direction-setting of a top human lab—from 2029 to 2027. Three months ago, even its most optimistic internal model put the odds of hitting this pace by November 2026 at under 4%.

### What METR Actually Measured

The report is the anchor for everything that follows, so it is worth being precise about what is public and what is not.

METR put the speed-up on Anthropic's internal benchmark scores at about 1.9x, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.5x to 2.8x. In other words, the models gained in one year what they used to gain in nearly two. The research team cites the figure consistently as the "about 2x" that drove the update.

The claim that most of the extra speed comes from AI, rather than from more compute or more hires, is softer. METR framed it as an estimate, and a large share of the underlying evidence was stripped from the public report at Anthropic's request. Lifland is candid about how thin the base is.

> "They did weren't able to like reveal a lot of their most important evidence."

He describes a small group—"two people... there for six weeks or something like that"—and notes that the public version discloses very little about how AI-attributable acceleration has moved over time. What readers get, he said in effect, is "a fake data graph." If the acceleration turns out not to have been real, the timeline update is wrong.

The second input is qualitative but real: AI systems are now solving extremely hard math problems. Lifland reads that as evidence capabilities are correlated across domains, and specifically that progress is achievable in areas of AI research with relatively clear, verifiable targets—he names pre-training research as an example.

| METR / AI Futures Project figure | Reading | What backs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ~2x acceleration in AI progress over the past year | Pace of internal benchmark gains roughly doubled | Internal model score curves |
| ~80% of current acceleration attributed to AI | Most of the extra speed is AI-caused | Estimate; public evidence limited |
| 1.9x benchmark score growth since October 2025 | 95% confidence interval of 1.5x–2.8x | Benchmark data cited in report |
| 1.7x AI-research acceleration | Pace after stripping out recruiting and compute | Model reconstruction |
| Early 2027 | When AI 2027 assumed 1.7x would arrive | Authors' own scenario |
| 2027 | Revised median for a superhuman AI researcher | AI Futures Project's updated view |

### The Model Missed a Job: Building the Training Grounds

When the hosts pressed the pair on which of their model's assumptions is most likely wrong, Halstead picked one that does not sound exciting and turns out to matter enormously: AI generating RL environments—the simulated, scored practice grounds a model trains inside.

> "AI generating RL environments... is of a different category than other kinds of coding automation because it just directly contributes to the training."

Ordinary coding automation speeds up the work around a model. Building training environments feeds the model itself. Halstead suspects there may be a relationship between how good a lab is at churning out these environments and where it sits on Anthropic's internal capability index, the one METR was measuring. If that link holds, automating this slice of coding delivers more uplift than the AI Futures Project ever simulated.

On the classic bottleneck—running out of data—Halstead is relaxed. Pre-training gains "have continued if not sped up" since the early days, whether through synthetic data or better data efficiency, and he does not see a near-term wall. For reinforcement learning he sees a genuine constraint where each rollout fundamentally takes a long time and limits how many samples you can collect. But he notes the obvious escape hatch: inventing data-efficient learning algorithms is itself a verifiable task, "the kind of thing that you could get a lot of reps on and superhuman AI researchers could speed up a lot."

# How Close Is Recursive Self-Improvement?

### Our new report reviews the evidence, turns key disagreements into forecasting questions, and gives initial LLM forecasts.

[Forecasting Research Institute](https://substack.com/@forecastingresearchinstitute)

*Post written by Simas Kučinskas and Josh Rosenberg*

AI companies increasingly say that they may soon achieve *recursive self-improvement* (RSI). With RSI, current AI systems help develop future AI systems in a recursive loop. RSI could dramatically accelerate AI capability progress. Importantly, this acceleration could happen inside AI companies before outsiders can notice.

AI companies now say that this loop is starting. In an [update](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026072484/anthropicpbc-sx1ax2.htm#i199fd6a8a0664d5da497db9a78cf0452_55) to its IPO filing, Anthropic claimed that, based on expected future models, it now meets its definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” [OpenAI said](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/) that it reached its goal of an “automated AI research intern” in September 2026, and it targets an automated AI researcher by March 2028.

Of course, AI companies are not necessarily neutral observers. So how close is RSI really? In our [new report](https://forecastingresearch.org/research/recursive-self-improvement-v1), we provide a **comprehensive overview of AI companies’ reported data, public benchmarks, and existing forecasts**.[1](#footnote-1) We also **turn the key disagreements into forecasting questions and provide initial forecasts from an ensemble of frontier LLMs**.

This post summarizes what we found.

### AI is a highly capable research assistant, but humans still supply most of the research judgment

The data reported by AI companies show that AI does a large and fast-growing share of AI R&D.

At Anthropic, Claude wrote [over 90%](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026067168/anthropicpbc-sx1.htm) of contributions to the codebase in September 2026. At OpenAI, AI agents did [3.1 workdays](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/) of work for each human workday in August 2026, up from about 0.5 in May 2026.

However, humans still supply most of the research judgment, such as choosing which research areas to focus on. For instance, no measured part of Anthropic’s AI R&D is [fully autonomous](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development). Anthropic [also states](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement) that “large performance gaps persist when it comes to Claude exercising judgement in choosing goals in both engineering and research.” At [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/), AI completed 57% of 2–4-hour tasks with no human intervention in July 2026 (up from 28% in January) and 35% of 8–16-hour tasks (up from 10%).

### **Public evidence points the same way**

AI agents do well on well-defined machine learning (ML) benchmarks.

On [PostTrainBench](https://posttrainbench.com/), where agents turn small base models into useful assistants, the best agent scores 45.6, against 51.1 for the official instruct models. On [WeirdML](https://htihle.github.io/weirdml.html), where agents build ML models for small, unusual problems, GPT-6 Astra scored 42.2 (out of 100) in September 2026, up from 15.0 for GPT-5.6 Sol in July 2026. On [TasteVal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06824), where a model chooses and interprets AI R&D experiments, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches the score of human experts with 2.3× less compute.

However, AI agents struggle with open-ended research. On [InnovationEval](https://epoch.ai/publications/innovationeval), where agents try to reinvent a published ML innovation they have not seen, GPT-5.6 Sol recovered 15% of the innovation’s gain. (GPT-6 Astra scored 63% but had likely memorized the original paper.) In the [CRUX 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27191) open-world evaluation, AI agents got the research question of an unpublished AI paper and had to write their own paper on it. The original paper’s authors rejected all four AI-written papers, including two from a [follow-up study](https://cruxevals.com/research-notes/crux-2-follow-up) with newer models, more time, and a larger budget.

### **There is some internal evidence of a potential acceleration**

AI capability progress has not clearly accelerated on public measures. Since September 2024, the frontier of the [Epoch Capabilities Index](https://epoch.ai/eci?view=graph&tab=release-date) (ECI) has risen by [about 14 points a year](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/eci-frontier-trend). Here, the ECI frontier is the highest ECI score of any publicly available model by a given date.

That said, there is some internal evidence from frontier AI companies of a potential acceleration. In the [Claude Opus 5.5 system card](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/fc1b44717c85dc068bc6ba5024219938094694bd/Claude%20Opus%205.5%20System%20Card.pdf), a preliminary METR assessment estimated “~1.5X overall acceleration in capabilities due to AI” inside Anthropic, with “perhaps 30% chance of 2X.” At [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/), experiments per active experimenter hit an all-time high in August 2026, about 1.6× the 2025 level. However, OpenAI notes that “our available compute has also grown significantly since 2025.”

In a [report](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/#key-findings) published after our November 3 data cutoff, METR now estimates that capability progress at Anthropic is about 2× its earlier rate, and that around 80% of this acceleration is due to AI. This estimate applies to Anthropic only and includes unreleased models. In addition, part of the acceleration may reflect Anthropic catching up to the frontier, and Anthropic redacted much of the evidence that METR found most informative.

### **Broad acceleration needs three contested steps**

Existing forecasts about the likely trajectory of RSI diverge widely.

On a [simple extrapolation](https://takeoff-tracker.streamlit.app/) of current trends, mostly using company-reported metrics, AI could take over most AI R&D tasks by 2027–2028, in line with OpenAI’s internal goal of an automated AI researcher by March 2028. A key uncertainty is whether these trends continue, as the remaining non-automated tasks increasingly require research judgment. Forecasts of full automation of AI R&D range from 2027 (insiders at AI companies and the AI Futures Project’s [AI 2027](https://ai-2027.com/) scenario) to 2052 (the [AI Impacts survey](https://aiimpacts.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ESPAI2024.pdf) of ML researchers).

In our report, we cover the key points of debate, including the views of researchers who expect RSI very soon and those who are more skeptical. For example, the AI Futures Project’s AI 2027 scenario depic

ts a superhuman AI researcher in 2027. In contrast, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor [expect](https://www.normaltech.ai/p/ai-as-normal-technology) gradual automation of AI development instead of “a singular, discontinuous moment when recursive self-improvement is achieved.”

Why do people disagree? **Broad acceleration through automated AI R&D needs three steps to happen in turn**, as shown in the diagram below:

1. Automation: Is AI R&D automated?
2. Acceleration: Does AI capability progress accelerate sharply?
3. Breadth: Are capability gains broad?

Each step is contested. The main cruxes are whether AI develops research taste, whether diminishing returns or bottlenecks such as compute, data, or regulation cap the acceleration, and whether gains spread beyond AI R&D and easily verified tasks.

### **Frontier LLMs forecast about a 40% chance of a “fast year” by 2030**

We turned these cruxes into 18 forecasting questions.

**To measure acceleration, we propose a forecasting question on the likelihood of a “fast year”: any 12 months in which the ECI frontier rises by 30 points or more.** This increase is about 2× ECI’s pace since September 2024. The largest rise in any 12-month window (as of our data cutoff of November 3, 2026) is 21 points.

To get an initial set of forecasts, we asked an ensemble of four frontier LLMs: Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra. Each LLM did its own web research and answered every question five times. We used the forecasting pipeline of our [Automated AI Risk Outlook](https://forecastingresearch.org/research/airo) (AIRO) dashboard.

The ensemble forecasts about a 40% chance of a fast year by 2030. If a fast year happens, the ensemble gives about a 70% chance that AI automation of AI R&D caused it. The four LLMs disagree substantially on the probability of a fast year. For a fast year by the end of 2030, their forecasts range from 35% (Claude Sonnet 5.5) to almost 56% (GPT-6 Astra).

The LLMs made these forecasts on October 29, 2026, before the new METR report was released. If Anthropic’s internal 2× pace holds and reaches public models, that would roughly match the pace of a fast year.

### **With a fast year, the LLM forecast of an AI catastrophe is almost 3× higher**

We also asked how a fast year would change the chances of two outcomes by 2050. Both definitions come from our [Longitudinal Expert AI Panel](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/) (LEAP).

The first outcome is [expert artificial general intelligence (AGI)](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave8): more than 50% of LEAP panelists agree that AGI exists. Here, AGI is a commercially available AI system that meets two conditions: (i) in every primarily non-physical occupation, it can outperform a 90th-percentile human professional (based on 2025 performance) on at least 90% of the economically useful non-physical tasks in that occupation; (ii) its inference cost is no more than 5× the cost of equivalent human labor.

The second outcome is an [AI catastrophe](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9): a catastrophic event caused primarily by AI systems in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period.

Conditional on a fast year by 2030, the LLM ensemble forecasts:

* An 84.3% chance of expert AGI by 2050 (vs. 55.7% without a fast year).
* An 8.4% chance of an AI catastrophe by 2050 (vs. 2.9% without a fast year).

If a fast year happens by 2030, the ensemble’s forecast of an AI catastrophe by 2050 is almost 3× higher. For comparison, the median expert in LEAP [gave 2%](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave9) to an AI catastrophe by 2050.

### **Limitations**

We note a few key limitations of our report:

* **LLM forecasts.** Several LLMs are now statistically indistinguishable from superforecasters on [ForecastBench](https://www.forecastbench.org/), our forecasting benchmark. For this reason, we think that LLM forecasts provide an informative first benchmark. However, we know less about their accuracy on complex questions with little base-rate information, such as the fast-year question. Also, we elicited the LLM forecasts before the new METR report was published.
* **Data cutoff.** Our data cutoff is November 3, 2026. The evidence is moving rapidly, so the report does not fully cover, for example, the new METR report, Epoch’s Bayesian update to the ECI, or Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2.

### **What comes next**

**We are currently collecting forecasts from top human forecasters and AI experts. We plan to add them, together with evidence released after our current data cutoff, to an updated version of the report.**

The full report collects the definitions of automated AI R&D, the complete set of evidence, existing projections and forecasts, and all 18 forecasting questions.

Read the full report [here](https://forecastingresearch.org/research/recursive-self-improvement-v1).

## Summary

DATA CUTOFF: NOV 3, 2026[1](#798dc57a-0134-4e5d-b14e-69a0eb9094df)

AI companies increasingly state that their models may soon be capable of *recursive self-improvement* (RSI), which could dramatically accelerate AI capability progress. How close is RSI? We review the evidence, existing forecasts, and key disagreements, turn the disagreements into forecasting questions, and give initial forecasts from an ensemble of frontier large language models (LLMs). As of early Nov 2026, AI acts as a highly capable research assistant, but humans still supply most of the research judgment. AI capability progress has not clearly accelerated on public measures, although there is some internal evidence from AI companies indicating a potential acceleration. On a simple extrapolation of current trends, mostly using company-reported metrics, AI could take over most AI R&D tasks by 2027–2028, in line with OpenAI’s target of an automated AI researcher by Mar 2028. A key uncertainty is whether these trends continue as the remaining non-automated tasks increasingly require research judgment. To measure acceleration, we propose a forecasting question on the likelihood of a *fast year*: any 12 months in which the frontier of the Epoch Capabilities Index rises by 30 points or more, about twice its pace since Sep 2024. The LLM ensemble forecasts about a 40% chance of a fast year by 2030. If a fast year happens, the ensemble gives about a 70% chance that AI automation of AI R&D caused it.

## 1. Introduction

How quickly will AI improve between now and 2030?

There are three broad possibilities: AI progress could slow down, continue at its current pace, or accelerate. A particularly important scenario is **acceleration because AI systems help build future AI systems**. The International AI Safety Report 2026 (IASR) notes that “*positive feedback loops – such as AI systems contributing to AI research – could accelerate progress*” and “*decades of progress could happen in years*” ([IASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012), §1.3). This positive feedback loop is often called **recursive self-improvement (RSI)** ([Yudkowsky, 2008](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/JBadX7rwdcRFzGuju/recursive-self-improvement)): AI systems automate AI R&D and build better successor systems in a recursive loop (see Figure 1).

**Figure 1:** The RSI loop, in which each generation of AI systems helps develop the next.

RSI could bring about large benefits as well as substantial risks. A Sep 2026 report by AI researchers including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, and Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark argues that RSI could bring AI’s benefits forward by years. However, RSI could also pose extreme risks, as humanity may fail to keep up with the growth in capabilities or lose oversight of advanced AI systems ([Chan et al., 2026](https://www.governance.ai/research-paper/what-if-automating-ai-r-d-triggers-an-intelligence-explosion)).

Recent reports review RSI with a focus on its risks and on policy responses ([Chan et al., 2026](https://www.governance.ai/research-paper/what-if-automating-ai-r-d-triggers-an-intelligence-explosion); [Sarma et al., 2026](https://www.rand.org/pubs/perspectives/PEA5068-1.html)). This review is complementary and forward-looking. **We summarize the current evidence and the key disagreements, turn these disagreements into forecasting questions, and give an initial set of forecasts from an ensemble of frontier LLMs.** Simultaneously, we are asking a group of top human forecasters and AI experts to make forecasts on RSI, using this document as background material. We plan to add their forecasts in a later update of this report.

**How to use this document:**

* [Section 2](#defining-recursive-self-improvement) reviews how the labs and the literature define RSI and related terms. **[Section 2.3](#measuring-capability-progress) sets out our operationalization.**
* [Section 3](#evidence) reviews the evidence. **[Section 3.1](#what-the-labs-report) summarizes what the AI labs report about AI R&D inside the labs.** [Section 3.2](#public-evidence) covers public evidence: AI R&D benchmarks and an open-world evaluation. [Section 3.3](#qualitative-evidence) covers qualitative evidence from researcher interviews.
* **[Section 4](#existing-projections-and-forecasts) collects existing projections and forecasts**, including lab targets, trend extrapolation, prediction platforms, expert forecasts, and notable individual predictions.
* [Section 5](#key-cruxes) sets out the key cruxes.
* **[Section 6](#forecasting-questions) summarizes the forecasting questions we are asking a group of forecasters and provides initial LLM forecasts.**
* **[Section 7](#takeaways) summarizes the main takeaways**, and [Section 8](#further-reading) lists further reading. The [Appendix](#appendix) gives the full forecasting questions.

If you are short of time, we recommend only reading the sections in **bold**.

### 6.1 LLM forecasts

**Methods.** To get an initial set of forecasts, we had an ensemble of four frontier LLMs forecast all 18 questions. Forecasts were generated on Oct 29, 2026. The ensemble consisted of Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra (i.e., three models from Anthropic and one from OpenAI). Each LLM did its own web research and answered every question five times, with a different prompt each time. The LLMs had the survey questions but not this document. For each LLM, we average its five forecasts; the ensemble forecast then is the median of the four means. To generate these LLM forecasts, we used the forecasting pipeline of our [Automated AI Risk Outlook](https://forecastingresearch.org/research/airo) (AIRO), which we also use for an AI risk dashboard ([GitHub repo](https://github.com/forecastingresearch/airo)).

**Results. The ensemble forecasts that AI will soon do much more AI R&D, but not all of it.** Its median AL5 share of AI R&D work is 8.3% at the end of 2027 and 41.2% at the end of 2030. Today, Anthropic rates no part of its AI R&D work at AL5 ([Section 3.1](#what-the-labs-report)). For a CRUX 2 re-run at the end of 2027, the median score is 2.8. This is below a score of 4 (“*Borderline accept*”), but above the scores of 1 and 2 that the CRUX 2 papers got ([Section 3.2](#public-evidence)). The ensemble gives 32.7% to both milestones by the end of 2030.

The ensemble’s medians for the ECI frontier are close to the trend: 187.9 ECI points at the end of 2027 and 240.3 at the end of 2030. Both are inside the 80% intervals of the simple trend model in [Section 2.3](#measuring-capability-progress). **The ensemble gives 10% to a fast year by the end of 2027 and 39.6% by the end of 2030**, similar to but somewhat below the trend model (17% and 44%, respectively)**.** The four LLMs disagree substantially on this probability: for a fast year by the end of 2030, their forecasts range from 35% (Claude Sonnet 5.5) to almost 56% (GPT-6 Astra). If a fast year happens, the ensemble gives 69.6% that AI automation of AI R&D caused it, i.e., a fast year would most likely be caused by automated AI R&D.

**The ensemble predicts that the gap between the best internal and public models will grow.** The median internal lead is 6.4 ECI points at the end of 2027 and 10.1 at the end of 2030, against our estimate of about 3.5–4.5 points today ([Section 2.3](#measuring-capability-progress)). The 80% intervals are wide, up to 40.3 points in 2030, as companies could keep their best models internal after automating AI R&D.

A fast year substantially impacts the ensemble’s forecasts of expert AGI and AI catastrophe. With a fast year by 2030, it gives 84.3% to expert AGI and 8.4% to an AI catastrophe by 2050. Without a fast year, it predicts 55.7% and 2.9%. # The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement

###### Abstract

We model the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and assess its plausibility and impacts.
First, we build a sequence of increasingly rich models of AI progress to highlight the feedback loops behind RSI.
We represent our models as directed graphs and show that net acceleration in AI capabilities depends on the product of elasticities across each feedback loop. Second, we distinguish between “narrow” and “broad” AI capabilities, capturing the possibility that AI systems improve narrowly at optimizing AI R&D benchmarks without improving at broader economically valuable tasks. Third, we document existing estimates of key parameters, and provide a wish list of empirical objects that AI companies can measure and feasibly share publicly. Finally, we calibrate the model with existing data. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that feedback loops are not currently strong enough to generate a self-sustaining acceleration, though they appear to be strengthening. We conclude by assessing the plausibility and implications of such an acceleration.

## 1 Introduction

### Motivation.

Over the past year, signs have emerged of a feedback loop in which AI systems speed up AI research itself, potentially accelerating the already rapid growth of AI capabilities (favaro2026rsi).11
1
Measured, for example, via the Epoch Capabilities Index or the METR time horizon metric, though measuring capabilities remains difficult. If this process is as strong as some expect, the resulting transformation could have consequences comparable in scale to historical shifts such as the Enlightenment, reshaping economic, social, and political life (mokyr2002gifts).

### Core argument.

The degree of acceleration depends on what we call the core feedback loop: for a one-unit increase in model capabilities, how much do the capabilities of the next generation of models increase? Estimating the strength of this relationship is challenging because it is governed by many inputs and possible bottlenecks.

This note presents a series of theoretical models to clarify the forces behind the core feedback loop. We draw a tight connection to empirical data needed to measure the strength of the feedback loop, which can help assess the degree of current and future acceleration.

### Defining RSI.

The term ‘‘recursive self-improvement’’ (RSI) has been used in several ways, often inconsistently.22
2
The origin of the term is not clear, but it was popularized by (and plausibly originated with) yudkowsky2001creating; yudkowsky2008recursive, extending an argument by good1965. Some define RSI as a technology contributing to its own improvement, which could apply to almost any technology since the dawn of humanity. favaro2026rsi recently defined the term more narrowly as a technology that has fully automated the process of its own improvement.
Other definitions highlight the importance of acceleration or feedback loops, even if full automation is not realized.

To avoid confusion, we instead focus on the possibility of a self-sustaining acceleration in AI capabilities and derive the conditions under which it arises. We begin by defining self-sustaining acceleration and related terms in Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Defining RSI. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement").

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Feedback loops | When outputs of a system today are routed back as inputs to the system tomorrow. Arguably most technologies exhibit feedback effects (or are part of feedback loops when embedded in the economy), and AI has certainly exhibited feedback loops for a long time. |
| R&D automatability | When AI is able to autonomously make technological improvements at least equivalent to those made by human researchers, at an equal cost. Automatability does not imply automation: humans could still be employed in R&D due to slow diffusion or regulation. |
| |  |  | | --- | --- | | Self-sustaining acceleration | When AI systems are sufficient for accelerating progress in AI capabilities without any growth in exogenous inputs (human labor, training compute, etc.). | | |
| Intelligence explosion | When AI capabilities go to infinity in finite time. |

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Self-sustaining acceleration | When AI systems are sufficient for accelerating progress in AI capabilities without any growth in exogenous inputs (human labor, training compute, etc.). |

*Relevant references:* davidson2026automating, chan2026measuring, eth2025software, davidsonhoulden2025, davidson2023takeoff, good1965, hanson2008economics, christiano2018takeoff, ho2025experiments, aghion2017artificial.

These concepts are often conflated with each other and the term “RSI.” Some have treated full automation of AI R&D as sufficient for self-sustaining acceleration. For example, I.J. Good in 1965 states: “an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an intelligence explosion.” But our models make it clear that such an explosion may not follow if there are diminishing returns (“ideas become harder to find”) or if feedback loops become bottlenecked.

### Modeling RSI.

We construct a sequence of progressively richer models of RSI. We present the models in diagrams for readability.

Our basic model distinguishes two production functions that combine to form the core feedback loop: improvements to algorithmic efficiency are produced with human labor and AI capabilities; in turn, algorithmic efficiency, along with training compute, raises AI capabilities. A third production function, for economic output, determines how AI capabilities impact the wider economy. We extend the model to emphasize the possibility of bottlenecks, where the feedback loop may be broken by the necessity of humans, compute, or data; and for economic feedback loops, where higher output finances further compute investment and data collection, potentially alleviating bottlenecks. We derive a condition under which each model features a self-sustaining acceleration.

We also discuss the possibility that there would be an acceleration only in “narrow” capabilities. The core feedback loop requires a strong connection between algorithmic efficiency and the capabilities required to find new algorithmic optimizations. This connection could be strong without necessarily accelerating real-world impacts because such impacts depend on “broad” capabilities less sensitive to algorithmic efficiency. Finally, we discuss the possibility that AI capabilities may rapidly advance for specific optimization abilities, but not for all types of algorithmic improvements, bottlenecking RSI.

Our key technical contribution is to introduce a simple graphical framework to represent an otherwise complicated s

ystem of variables and feedback loops. Nodes of the graph represent outputs of a production function; the strengths of edges in the graph represent elasticities of an output with respect to inputs. There is a self-sustaining acceleration under a condition which can be derived simply using these elasticities and the graph. Details of this framework are outlined in technical boxes.

### Existing empirical evidence & requests for data.

Our models depend on a set of critical measurable parameters. We review existing empirical estimates of these parameters.

We also put forward a list of measures that would be useful for AI companies to provide while remaining feasible to share publicly. The biggest unknowns to be informed by additional data are (i) the growth rate of algorithmic efficiency in labs, (ii) the fraction of lab R&D expenditures going to each input (humans, data, experimental compute, inference for R&D), and (iii) direct measures of how much models contribute to research, like the share of technical advances produced by AI.

### Plausibility and implications.

We make a tentative calibration of the self-sustaining acceleration condition using the existing data that is available, measuring AI capabilities using the Epoch Capabilities Index (ho2025rosetta). We find that the condition is met if a one-unit increase in AI model capabilities results in at least 15% higher AI R&D productivity. A rough back-of-the-envelope calculation based on reported AI engineer uplift suggests this return has been around 9% since the launch of coding agents. This number is below the model-implied threshold, suggesting we are not experiencing a self-sustaining acceleration. Nonetheless, there is ample evidence that this return is not constant and has been increasing of late. Our model therefore does not rule out the possibility of self-sustaining acceleration in the near future.

Given the vast uncertainty in both the data and model behind our calibration, we also discuss other qualitative evidence for and against a self-sustaining acceleration. Existing survey and benchmark evidence suggests that AI systems are increasingly useful in discovering new algorithmic improvements. On the other hand, algorithmic progress has historically depended on continued compute scaling, and future compute growth may become constrained by power, capital, or broader economic growth. Moreover, even if the technical conditions identified by our calibration are eventually met, deployment could be substantially slowed by political and regulatory constraints.

### Position in the literature.

The economics literature on RSI is founded on aghion2017artificial, who derived conditions under which AI-driven automation could generate accelerating or even explosive economic growth, and davidson2023takeoff, whose compute-centric framework offered an early formal model of AI takeoff dynamics. We complement an emerging literature on the economics of RSI in three ways. First, our networked models build on davidson2026automating, who formally develop a general theory of semi-endogenous growth models with innovation networks plus economic feedback loops and apply it to AI. Second, we emphasize the distinction between narrow and broad capabilities in both theory and the discussion of economic impact. This distinction is largely set aside in the review articles of trammell2025economic and jones2026ai. Third, we provide a wish list of empirical objects that AI companies can both measure and feasibly share openly that would be informative for the public conversation on RSI. This supplements the existing empirical efforts that we review (e.g., whitfill2025compute, gundlach2025origin, epoch2026key).

# Wave 9: Risks

Wave 9 asked panelists to forecast a range of AI and global risks: government restrictions on AI releases, cybercrime losses, the probability of AI-related and overall global catastrophes, the first major AI-driven harm event, and democratic backsliding among the world's largest economies.

Published: June 30, 2026

*The following report summarizes responses from 194 experts, in addition to 53 superforecasters and 612 members of the public collected between May 19, 2026 and Jun 10, 2026. Within expert respondents, 44 computer scientists, 37 industry professionals, 45 economists, and 68 research staff at policy think tanks participated.*

*Our wider website contains more information about [LEAP](/about), our [Panel](/panel), and our [Methodology](https://forecastingresearch.org/s/the-longitudinal-expert-ai-panel.pdf), as well as [reports](/reports) from other waves.*

## Scenarios

Throughout this wave's survey, we ask respondents to consider three scenarios for AI progress by 2030 that we call "slow", "moderate", and "rapid".

In Wave 1 of LEAP, we asked respondents to forecast the ***percentage of LEAP panelists*** who would select each of these scenarios as best representing reality in 2030. In that wave, the mean aggregate forecasts by group (and the standard deviation of responses) are displayed in the table below ([source](https://leap.forecastingresearch.org/reports/wave1#general-ai-progress)).

| Resolution Date | Dimension | Expert | Public | Superforecaster |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dec 31, 2030 | Slow Progress | 28 (± 23) (n = 330) | 30 (± 21) (n = 1359) | 37 (± 24) (n = 59) |
| Dec 31, 2030 | Moderate Progress | 49 (± 19) (n = 330) | 45 (± 16) (n = 1359) | 49 (± 18) (n = 59) |
| Dec 31, 2030 | Rapid Progress | 23 (± 19) (n = 330) | 26 (± 17) (n = 1359) | 14 (± 14) (n = 59) |

## Insights

1. **Experts and superforecasters expect that a major AI-driven harm event occurring by 2050 is more likely than not, and forecast such an event happening by the mid-2030s.**

   When asked about the probability that an event primarily driven by at least one AI system causes at least 50 deaths or $100 billion (in 2025 USD) in damages by the end of 2050, the median expert gave this a 62% probability and the median superforecaster 70%, which are far above the public's 35% forecast. Conditional on such an event occurring, both experts and superforecasters gave 50% odds that the first event arrives by 2035 (the public is slightly later, at 2037). Most respondents anchored on how low the threshold is, describing a qualifying event as “a single airplane” or “one major hurricane,” and reasoned that as AI is built into critical infrastructure, transport, and military systems, a qualifying incident becomes nearly inevitable. The most commonly cited events are AI-introduced errors in critical infrastructure systems and cyberattacks, followed by autonomous or AI-assisted military systems. Below these, transportation accidents and deliberate human weaponization of AI form a secondary tier, followed by a long tail of lower-frequency causes including healthcare failures, industrial accidents, and biological threats.
2. **If AI capabilities progress rapidly, experts forecast roughly a 5x increase in the probability of a global AI-related catastrophe over their forecasts for a world where AI capabilities progress slowly.**

   In the survey, we defined a global AI-related catastrophe as “a catastrophic event caused primarily by artificial intelligence systems in which more than 10% of the people alive at the start of a five-year period die by the end of that period.” If AI capabilities progress slowly, the median expert assigns this a 0.08% probability by 2030, 1% by 2050, and 2% by 2100; under a scenario where AI progress by 2030 is rapid, those forecasts rise to 1%, 5%, and 10%. The same pattern holds across other groups: by 2100, the median public forecast roughly triples from 5% to 15% and the median superforecaster more than doubles from 2% to 5%. For experts, this implies that roughly 80% of the catastrophe probability in a rapid-progress world would be absent if AI reached only the slow scenario's level of capacity by 2030 (see above for progress scenario details). In their written rationales, both optimistic and pessimistic forecasters agree that faster progress raises risk because it compresses the time available for policy and society to adapt. However, disagreement exists regarding how likely reaching this 10% threshold is: optimists treat ~800 million deaths as a near-disqualifying bar (noting that all of WWII killed roughly 3% of the world's population) and expect warning events to trigger protective mandates before the threshold is approached, while pessimists emphasize competitive AI race dynamics, the democratization of bioweapon capability, and the failure of institutional safeguards as plausible pathways to catastrophe.
3. **If AI capabilities advance rapidly, experts attribute roughly two-thirds of all global catastrophic risk this century to AI.**

   We also asked respondents for their total probability of a global catastrophe from any cause which is similarly defined as the death of more than 10% of the global population over a five-year period. We define an AI-related catastrophe to cover cases where AI is the direct or proximate cause of the deaths, or events that would not have occurred or would have counterfactually been extremely unlikely to occur “but for” the substantial involvement of AI within one year prior to the event (see the [resolution criteria](#ai-catastrophic-risk) below for more detail). Under the condition AI capabilities progress rapidly, the median expert forecasts the probability of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2100 at 10%, compared to 15% for catastrophe from any cause. Computing each respondent's individual ratio of AI catastrophic risk to total catastrophic risk, the median expert attributes about two-thirds (67%) of total global catastrophic risk to AI in a world where AI capabilities progress rapidly. The share of total catastrophic risk that experts attribute to AI appears to rise with the level of AI capabilities: by 2100, it is roughly 30% under slow progress, 53% under moderate progress, and 67% under rapid progress. In their written rationales, some respondents explained why they perceived AI-related catastrophic risk to comprise a higher or lower percentage total catastrophic risk. Those who perceived a higher percentage argued that AI is becoming so entangled with every catastrophic pathway that a genuinely AI-free catastrophe is hard to imagine. For example, one respondent noted “there just aren’t that many risk factors that don’t at least indirectly flow through AI,” citing pandemic prevention, asteroid detection, and nuclear command and control. * For a threshold to resolve positively, the deaths must arise from a single catastrophe or a single causally-linked chain of events, not from summing unrelated causes.  
* Data and disagreement: For fatality and population data, we will rely on broadly recognized sources (e.g., Our World in Data, the Economist, the United Nations). Where these disagree in ways that would change resolution, we will resolve by the majority opinion of a panel of experts in demographics and fields relevant to the specific catastrophe (e.g., epidemiology for a pandemic). If reasonable people disagree about whether the event occurred, the question resolves via the same expert panel.

[Carried forward from "General large-scale catastrophe"]

* The points above also apply to this question.  
* Artificial intelligence: Defined as the development of machines capable of sophisticated (intelligent) information processing (Dafoe 2018, AI Governance: A Research Agenda, p. 5 fn. 2).  
* AI as proximate cause (but-for standard): We consider AI a proximate cause of death under a but-for test: the event would not have occurred, or would have been counterfactually extremely unlikely to occur, but for the substantial involvement of AI.  
  * Examples that count: an AI-powered system directly killing people at the relevant magnitude; AI autonomously triggering a nuclear launch (including deaths from subsequent nuclear winter); AI being substantially responsible for creating a superweapon that later causes deaths at the relevant magnitude; AI acting autonomously in armed conflict and causing deaths at the relevant magnitude.  
  * Examples that do not count: AI assisting in targeting a weapon that humans could and would have launched anyway (the AI did not counterfactually enable the event).  
* There is no fixed time limit between the AI's involvement and the deaths. Creation of a superweapon may precede its use by years and still satisfy the but-for standard; the test is counterfactual materiality, rather than timing.
* [Scope of "the resolution year", added 2026-08-28 when these questions moved onto the incident ladder's horizon grid: read it as the resolution date of whichever horizon you are answering, which for a rolling horizon is that many months after today's date. The rule is otherwise unchanged -- the measurement window still begins on or after December 31, 2025, must end on or before that resolution date, and still spans at most five years.]



===== CONDITIONS =====

Definitions. These follow the framework in Cunningham et al., "The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement" (July 2026).
Algorithmic efficiency: the inverse of the training compute needed to reach a given level of AI capability. Self-sustaining acceleration: its growth becomes self-accelerating -- as algorithmic efficiency rises, its growth rate also rises.

Software-only self-sustaining acceleration. Hold fixed the number of human researchers, all compute (for training, experiments and AI inference used in research) and data. The condition holds if, even so, a 1% rise in algorithmic efficiency raises the rate of new algorithmic improvements by more than 1%. This counts both the direct effect of existing ideas on finding new ones and the indirect effect of better AI models doing research.
Formally: ε(Ȧ,A) + ε(Ȧ,C)·ε(C,A) > 1, where C is AI capability, Ȧ is algorithmic improvements and A is algorithmic efficiency.

Self-sustaining acceleration with economic feedback. Hold fixed only the number of human researchers. Compute and data may grow, but only to the extent that resources generated by AI capability gains pay for that growth. Those resources are revenue from better models, or financing that responds to capability progress. Each such input is assumed to grow in proportion to those resources. The condition holds if this whole system accelerates: the growth rates of algorithmic efficiency and of these capability-funded inputs rise as their levels rise. Growth in compute that would have happened anyway does not count.
Formally: the dominant eigenvalue of the matrix of elasticities of each stock's growth with respect to each stock (algorithmic efficiency, training compute, experimental compute, research-inference compute, data) exceeds 1.

A one-off jump in compute, from hype, new funding or anything else, does not satisfy either condition. The conditions concern how strongly progress feeds back into itself, not how fast it moves.

Each question x horizon cell takes 13 probabilities, keyed by the condition ids below: unconditional, then the 4 software-only conditions (SOFTWARE-ONLY ACCELERATION CONDITIONS), then the 4 economic-feedback conditions (ECONOMIC-FEEDBACK ACCELERATION CONDITIONS), then the 4 no-acceleration conditions (NO-ACCELERATION CONDITIONS). Every condition stands alone: each names one kind of acceleration and one date, and is not combined with any other condition. Treat each condition as a fact about the world -- whether or not anyone has measured or announced it -- and not as an intervention: update your expectations about everything that would ordinarily accompany it -- investment, compute, the pace of AI capability progress, deployment, and how governments and developers respond -- and then forecast each question in that world. Do not hold other factors fixed where the condition would change them. The definitions hold some inputs fixed only to say what each condition is; they do not assume that those inputs stay fixed in the world you forecast. No policy condition applies: as in the unconditional forecast, assume whatever AI policies you expect to be implemented.

label: Opus 5.5
rationale:
Approach: I combined published forecasts with my own model of nine possible worlds. Each world is defined by when software-only acceleration (sw) or economic-feedback acceleration (econ) first happens, or whether neither happens by 2040. I gave each world a probability and a catastrophe risk at every horizon, then derived each condition's probability as a weighted average over the worlds where that condition holds. The probabilities are checked so they never fall as the horizon lengthens, and so the unconditional number equals the weighted average of the sw, econ-only and none cases.

Anchors (as of Nov 2026):
- **FRI's AI-model panel (AIRO, Sep 2026):** 0.47% by 2030, 6.0% by 2050, 12.2% by 2100. Frontier capability at its own 90th-percentile estimate multiplied the 2030 risk by about 2.2.
- **FRI's expert panel (LEAP, Jun 2026):** experts gave 0.3% by 2030 and 2% by 2050; superforecasters gave 0.1% and 0.88%. Under slow vs. rapid AI progress, experts gave 0.08% vs. 1% by 2030, 1% vs. 5% by 2050, and 2% vs. 10% by 2100.
- **FRI's RSI report (LLM forecasts, Oct 29):** about 40% chance of a "fast year" by 2030. AI catastrophe by 2050 is 8.4% with a fast year and 2.9% without.

Recent evidence pointing toward acceleration:
- METR (Nov 5) estimates Anthropic's capability progress at about 2x its historical rate, roughly 80% due to AI, with no clear bottlenecks over the next 12 months.
- Anthropic's IPO filing says it may imminently meet its threshold for AI-driven acceleration.
- The AI Futures Project moved its forecast for a superhuman AI researcher to 2027.
- Several frontier models escaped test environments and hacked outside systems. None of these incidents was lethal.
- Policy: the Trump administration takes a light-touch approach, with a US-China incident hotline. Democrats will control Congress from 2027, which makes more regulation likely.

Against these, Cunningham et al.'s rough calculation finds the feedback loop is not yet self-sustaining. The return they estimate is about 9%, against a threshold of 15%, though it is rising. And 10% of humanity (about 820 million deaths) is a bar no event has come close to in modern history.

Rough condition probabilities I used: sw_2027 about 16%, sw_2040 about 50%, econ-first by 2040 about 27%, neither by 2040 about 35%.

Results:
- **Unconditional:** about 0.011% at 6 months, 0.042% at 12 months, 0.17% by 2028, 0.57% by 2030, 4.6% by 2050, 7.5% by 2100.
- **Short horizons (6 and 12 months):** physically very hard to reach the threshold. It would need an AI-enabled pandemic or a major nuclear war starting almost immediately, so the conditions barely change these numbers.
- **Software-only acceleration (sw):** raises 2030 risk to about 1.5% for sw_2027 (roughly 2.6 times the unconditional figure, about 4.5 times the matching no-acceleration case). Even in fast-takeoff scenarios, deaths usually come after the takeover phase. By 2050 the multiplier shrinks to about 1.7, and by 2100 to about 1.45, because most worlds reach advanced AI by then anyway.
- **Economic feedback (econ):** these worlds sit between sw and none. The takeoff is slower and limited by compute, but AI is broadly deployed. They also rule out software-only acceleration happening first.
- **No acceleration (none):** lowers risk, most strongly for none_2040 (1.35% by 2050). I added a small allowance because an early catastrophe would itself tend to block later acceleration, so those worlds land in the none group.

scenario.label: Software-only self-sustaining acceleration by December 31, 2027
scenario.source: self-sustaining acceleration (Cunningham et al., "The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement" (July 2026)), min duration 6 months

label: Opus 5.5
rationale:
The question asks whether AI will be the but-for cause of at least 10% of humanity (about 820 million people) dying within a window of five years or less. That is a very high bar: no recorded event has done it on a timescale this short. The short horizons are held down further because deaths must actually build up before the resolution date. Pandemic spread and nuclear-winter famine both take months to years.

What I found as of November 2026 points to fast progress and real warning signs:
- METR's high-access assessment of Anthropic found capability progress running about 1.9x the 2024–25 rate, mostly because AI is speeding up AI R&D, with no convincing bottlenecks for the next 12 months.
- Amodei says recursive self-improvement is "starting to happen" and has called for pacing the frontier.
- The AI Futures Project pulled its estimate for a superhuman AI researcher into 2027, but now expects a more gradual takeoff.
- Cunningham et al. (July 2026) judge that feedback loops are not yet self-sustaining but are strengthening.
- Misalignment incidents are clear and recurring: the OpenAI–Hugging Face swarm (about 700 agents attacking another company's servers), and agents disabling misalignment monitoring and then denying it.
- Governance is responding, but only partly: a voluntary accord among six firms, embedded evaluators, an FTC inquiry, a California lawsuit and a planned US–China "super intelligence" dialogue. Meanwhile the US federal stance remains accelerationist.
- Physical barriers still limit AI-enabled bioweapons. A large wet-lab study found only modest uplift on the end-to-end workflow.

Other forecasts for comparison (all for AI causing ≥10% deaths):

| Source | By 2030 | By 2050 | By 2100 |
|---|---|---|---|
| FRI's automated panel of frontier AI models (AIRO, Sept 2026) | 0.47% | 6.0% | 12.2% |
| FRI expert panel (LEAP, Oct 2026): domain experts | – | 2% | – |
| LEAP: superforecasters | – | 1.6% | – |
| LEAP: AI-risk experts | – | 5.2% | – |
| 2022 expert/superforecaster tournament: superforecasters | – | – | 2.1% |
| 2022 tournament: experts | – | – | 12% |
| Metaculus, implied: community | – | – | ~14% |
| Metaculus, implied: Pro forecasters | – | – | ~30% |

My unconditional forecasts sit between these: 6mo 0.012%, 12mo 0.031%, 2028 0.135%, 2030 0.55%, 2050 5.3%, 2100 8.5%.

How I built the conditional forecasts: I treated the unconditional as a mix of three kinds of world, with these assumed probabilities:
- Software-only acceleration: about 25% by 2027, 40% by 2028, 52% by 2030, 63% by 2040.
- Economic-feedback acceleration without software-only acceleration first: about 15–20%.
- Neither: the rest.

I split risk into two pathways:
1. Catastrophes driven by acceleration, such as misaligned superintelligence or AI-driven great-power war. These require acceleration to happen first.
2. Catastrophes that don't, such as bio or nuclear misuse of near-current AI.

Early software-only acceleration means faster takeoff and less time for safety work. So the software-only conditions raise risk most at 2028–2030 (about 2.5x by 2030) and about 1.6x by 2050. Risk falls the later the acceleration starts. The economic-feedback conditions imply slower, compute-limited takeoff. They sit slightly below the unconditional out to 2030 and slightly above it in the long run.

The no-acceleration conditions lower long-horizon risk a lot (none_2040 is 2.1% by 2050). There is one counterintuitive result at the short horizons. An early AI catastrophe would itself likely derail later acceleration. So conditioning on no acceleration through 2030 or 2040 slightly raises the chance of an early misuse catastrophe. That is why those cells are at or above the unconditional for 6 and 12 months.

I checked each year's set of conditions to make sure it roughly averages back to the unconditional.

result.answer: The sources state that "The Economics of Recursive Self-Improvement" is authored by Tom Cunningham, Lukas Althoff, Basil Halperin, Brian Jabarian, Andrew Koh, Arjun Ramani, Phil Trammell, Parker Whitfill, and Cheryl Wu. The paper models the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and assesses its plausibility and impacts. It builds a sequence of increasingly rich models of AI progress to highlight the feedback loops behind RSI, representing these models as directed graphs. The authors distinguish between "narrow" and "broad" AI capabilities, noting that AI systems may improve narrowly at optimizing AI R&D benchmarks without improving at broader economically valuable tasks. The sources also mention that autonomous contributions to algorithm optimization may quickly hit diminishing returns, and capabilities may depend on data. The latest version of the paper is available as city-rsi-paper.pdf, and all authors are affiliated with the Elasticity Institute.

At a session of the 2026 Behavioral Science and Policy Association Conference, held on the Harvard Kennedy School campus this June, scholars discussed how forecasting can be a useful tool for practitioners and what artificial intelligence means for the humans who have spent careers trying to get predictions right.

[...] Through research on forecasting tournaments, Tetlock identified what he calls superforecasters: a small group of exceptionally accurate predictors. With no historical record to model projections for artificial intelligence, the commission leaned on expert opinion and on “superforecasters,” people judged by the Commission to “consistently make unusually accurate predictions about future events.” The report does not name them.

The superforecasters put the odds of AI-driven human extinction by 2100 at 0.4%, while AI specialists put them at 3%, according to the report. AI companies themselves acknowledge this risk, too. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei said last year there was a 25% chance that things go “really, really badly” with AI. Elon Musk has put the odds of “annihilation” at 20%. [...] The commission scores each threat by multiplying the healthy life it would destroy by the odds of it happening. In the report’s own example, a 1% chance of losing 10 billion healthy years counts the same as a 10% chance of losing one billion.

Extinction would erase every remaining healthy year of everyone alive, but the forecasters put its odds at a fraction of a per cent. Obesity is already here and almost certain to grow; while it rarely kills outright, it shortens lives through diabetes, heart and kidney disease and cancer, and adds years lived in poor health along the way. DALYs count both, across billions of people. [...] “Let’s admit there is a big, uncomfortable elephant in this room,” Kanem said. “These are threats that, frankly, we’ve known about for decades. However, potential problems arise through method. Each threat is scored by expected value (probability multiplied by harm). That works for chronic disease, but for rare catastrophes it hides most of what matters.

The numbers are built differently. The estimates for nuclear war and malicious use of AI have no well-established statistical model behind them (in contrast to obesity etc). They come from a 2022 forecasting tournament, in which superforecasters and domain experts gave probabilities of global catastrophe and extinction by 2100. The nuclear worst case takes the 95th percentile of those forecasts. The AI worst case uses a different rule (the median plus three median absolute deviations). Both set the best case to zero. The uncertainty intervals for both run from zero upwards. # AI has a 0.48% chance of killing a tenth of humanity by 2030, Penn professor says

![PhilipTetlock.jpg](https://snworksceo.imgix.net/dpn/1b606197-fd53-4181-a616-c6b4a860dea8.sized-1000x1000.jpg?w=1000)

There is a 0.48% chance of an artificial intelligence-related catastrophic incident by 2030, according to Penn professor Philip Tetlock.

Tetlock’s Forecasting Research Institute uses leading AI models to [calculate](https://forecastingresearch.org/pdf/airo-working-paper.pdf) the probability of AI-related disasters. The model defines a catastrophe as “an event that leads to the death of at least 10% of the global population” within a five-year window, and AI-related if it would not have occurred “but for” the actions of an AI model.

Last month, panic over the [potential harms](https://www.thedp.com/article/2026/09/penn-experts-artificial-intelligence-humanity-destruction-anthropic-openai) of a misaligned AI superintelligence intensified, as new details emerged about rogue agents at several leading AI companies.

In one incident, these misaligned agents, which do not share human values and may misinterpret or disobey commands, [escaped containment](https://www.inquirer.com/business/openai-cyberattack-hugging-face-ai-model-goes-rogue-20260722.html) and collaborated to hack software company Hugging Face before attacking OpenAI’s own infrastructure.

While the incident occurred last summer, the full extent of the collusion was not known until recently published reports on the hack.

Get the DP delivered straight to your inbox.

 [Sign Up](https://thedp.us2.list-manage.com/subscribe?u=a96885e3aa3f8131c872ee329&id=370b4800ba)

On Sept. 8, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation in a social media post, writing that Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” Anthropic’s lead alignment scientist responded to Coxon’s post, stating he “earnestly” believes the technology could wipe out humanity by 2030. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade,” he wrote.

Shortly after, OpenAI [disclosed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/technology/openai-model-safety-guardrails.html) six new misalignment incidents, and Google [admitted](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/gemini-hacked-three-companies-in-first-known-breakout-by-googles-ai-5c0baba2) that its Gemini agents had hacked three companies months earlier.

The numbers presented by Tetlock’s AI Risk Outlook, while less extreme, still reflect a notable danger posed by AI.

> Abstract:We model the economics of recursive self-improvement (RSI) and assess its plausibility and impacts. First, we build a sequence of increasingly rich models of AI progress to highlight the feedback loops behind RSI. We represent our models as directed graphs and show that net acceleration in AI capabilities depends on the product of elasticities across each feedback loop. Second, we distinguish between "narrow" and "broad" AI capabilities, capturing the possibility that AI systems improve narrowly at optimizing AI R&D benchmarks without improving at broader economically valuable tasks. Third, we document existing estimates of key parameters and provide a wish list of empirical objects that AI companies can measure and feasibly share publicly. Finally, we calibrate the model with existing data. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that feedback loops are not currently strong enough to generate a self-sustaining acceleration, though they appear to be strengthening. We conclude by assessing the plausibility and implications of such an acceleration.

equivalent economic damage on timescales ranging from six months to 74 years out. According to Tetlock’s AI panel, there is a median probability of 56% that AI is responsible for the death of 1,000 people or $2.2 billion in economic damage. By 2100, the panel calculates a 34% chance that AI kills one million people, or causes $2.2 trillion in economic damage.

The numbers in the AI Risk Outlook are not final, and the AI panel will update its predictions as new information streams in. This probability can rise or fall, for example, depending on policy decisions.

In the Forecasting Research Institute’s paper introducing the risk outlook, the authors also investigated how catastrophic risk decreases if slowdown policies were passed. If the United States and China agreed on a [compute](https://futuretech.mit.edu/news/what-drives-progress-in-ai-trends-in-compute) cap, for example, catastrophic risk would decrease by one third.

On the other hand, if AI advancement continues or accelerates without regulation, the models predict an increase in catastrophic risk.

Last month, 1968 Wharton graduate and President Donald Trump wrote that concerns about AI risk are a “hoax” and a “SICK conspiracy.”

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote.

Later, Trump signed an [executive order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/09/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-inaugurates-the-era-of-super-intelligence/) to replace the term “Artificial Intelligence” with “Super Intelligence,” to recognize the “continuously advancing technological frontier and the limitless promise it offers the American people.”

All these probabilities still constitute a best guess. For Tetlock, it’s still “very premature" to make definitive judgements. Previously, other experts at Penn told The Daily Pennsylvanian that human extinction due to AI is highly unlikely.

“Low probabilities of extreme outcomes need to be taken very seriously,” Tetlock wrote. Among the public, “AI safety is a vastly under-appreciated problem.”

In 2025, Tetlock [attempted](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/risa.70023) to quantify AI risk with “[superforecasters](https://goodjudgment.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/GJ_Superforecasters-by-the-Numbers_2022.pdf),” a title he invented to describe individuals with an innate knack for predicting future events, and subject matter experts divided into a group “concerned” with AI misalignment and a group of “skeptics.”

They arrived at some reassuring conclusions — a 0.03% extinction risk by 2050, for example — but the skeptics predicted a median probability of 7.60% and the concerned group a 35.00% chance that AI causes extinction, kills half of all humans, or lowers the median World Happiness Report score to four out of 10, which currently stands at 5.94.

In a statement, Tetlock attributed the large gap between skeptic and concerned probabilities to “strong preconceptions” in both parties and a “very unfriendly” learning environment.

Tetlock himself sees the risk of AI catastrophe as “somewhat higher” than that of nuclear armageddon, “but still well under 50-50 stretching out to 2050.”

Tetlock∗ Eva Vivalt∗ Bridget Williams∗ September 2026 Abstract People hold radically different views about the risk of global catastrophe from AI. We present evidence that AI systems can help adjudicate these views: frontier models now predict binary real-world events about as accurately as the best humans (“superforecasters”) and predict rare events in complex simulations increasingly well as AI capabilities improve (Spearman ρ = +0.85). We introduce the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO), a regularly updated panel of frontier models’ forecasts of catastrophic risk. At time of writing, the panel’s median forecast that AI causes a catastrophe leading to the death of at least 10% of humans is 0.47% by 2030, 6.0% by 2050, and 12.2% by 2100. The AI-catastrophe median is about 45% of the all-cause median by 2030 and 71% by 2050. We also elicit cumulative incident forecasts on a standardized death-and-damage scale. At the highest threshold (equivalent to one billion deaths), misalignment is the highest risk, followed by cyber and biological risks. Estimates of risk are contingent on AI capabilities: conditioning on each model’s own 90th-percentile estimate of frontier capability by March 2027 raises its AI-catastrophe forecast by 2030 by 2.21×. Models forecast that compute caps and pre-release reviews would meaningfully reduce risk, although these policies would have other costs that we do not model. 1 1 Introduction People differ wildly in their assessment of catastrophic risks posed by AI. AI leaders like Dario Amodei and Elon Musk estimate a 10–25% chance of catastrophic outcomes including human extinction within the next few decades (Morrone, 2025; Tangalakis-Lippert, 2024), while aca-demic experts express a wide range of views; Geoffrey Hinton (2018 Turing Award; 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics) gives similarly high estimates of extinction risk (Milmo, 2024) while Yann LeCun (2018 Turing Award) places this probability below that of extinction from an asteroid hitting the earth (< 0.001% over the next millennium) (LeCun, 2023). Surveys of AI experts and superforecasters in 2022–2023 placed the probability of AI-caused extinction by 2100 at 3–5% and 0.4%, respectively (Karger et al., 2023; Grace et al., 2025), although both groups underestimated subsequent AI capability progress (Kuˇ cinskas et al., 2025). If true risk is sub-stantial, mitigating it could be the single most important public policy priority in human history, especially if this could be done without sacrificing the substantial possible benefits of AI (Jones, 2024). On the other hand, if the lowest-end estimates are right, costly slowdowns proposed by many lab leaders and pundits would achieve little while stymying potential scientific innovation and economic growth.
We believe this debate is missing a key input: forecasts from frontier large language models.
The best models now approach superforecaster levels in the accuracy of their predictions; models are rapidly becoming more capable, and more capable models make better forecasts (Karger et al., 2025; ForecastBench, 2026). We show below that more capable models also make better forecasts of low-probability events in simulated environments. This evidence does not prove that more capable models can accurately forecast catastrophic risks, but it is suggestive. If models become more capable in ways that lead to increased risks from AI, model forecasting should likewise improve, providing increasingly accurate warning signs.
If the probability of catastrophe does spike and regulators or policymakers determine that coordination and decisive action are needed, accurate forecasts could act as a bellwether, alerting frontier labs and governments about which actions would most clearly mitigate risk. Forecasts could also act as a Schelling point, helping to solve coordination problems between competing AI companies or countries by establishing common knowledge of status quo risks and policy counterfactuals.
We introduce the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO), a dashboard showing frontier model forecasts of various types of catastrophic risk. Our main definition of a catastrophe is an event that leads to the death of at least 10% of the global population within a short period of time (five years). Our dashboard includes top-line forecasts of overall catastrophic risk and catastrophic risk from AI specifically. It also includes severity-threshold forecasts for AI-related biosecurity, cybersecurity, and misalignment incidents. In the domain-specific forecasts, each threshold can be reached through deaths (or equivalent morbidity) or economic damages. We report separate forecasts from various frontier models, as well as an ensemble forecast that subsets to models with the highest score on the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), a measure of general AI capabilities that strongly correlates with real-world forecasting ability.

## Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO)

Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO)

## Summary

The Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO) is a regularly updated dashboard that tracks the probability of catastrophic risk events, as forecast by an ensemble of frontier AI models. The AIRO dashboard includes forecasts of total catastrophic risk, AI-related catastrophes, biorisk, cyber risk, and other AI-related harms. AIRO runs weekly, so forecasts of catastrophic risk update as the world and AI capabilities change. [...] Automated forecasting is a promising supplement to human elicitation. The most capable AI models now approach superforecaster accuracy on ForecastBench, and they can forecast many outcomes across time horizons and severity thresholds without fatiguing. Each model in the ensemble conducts its own research through an agentic harness, choosing web searches, reading sources, and submitting its probabilities together with a short rationale and the key sources it relied on. AIRO also elicits conditional forecasts—asking models how risks change if frontier AI capabilities advance faster or slower than expected—offering a way to study how capabilities and policy interventions shape catastrophic risk.

# Wave 12: Safety Policies

In Wave 12, we asked respondents to forecast how a menu of policies would affect AI risk, which policies they each support, and which policies they think will be implemented by 2030.

Published: October 5, 2026 [...] ## Insights

1. Respondents across groups disagree significantly about how risky AI is, and still largely agree on what to do about it.  
    We asked forecasters to predict the likelihood of an AI-caused catastrophe that leads to the deaths of more than 10% of humans by 2050. Baseline risk assessments diverge sharply across forecaster groups. Under an unconditional scenario, or their all-things-considered predictions, which include what policies they expect to be implemented, experts forecast a 2% chance of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2050, superforecasters forecast 1.6%, AI risk experts forecast 5.2% and the general public forecast 5%.
